events.title: Nvidia gave its first-ever year-ahead forecast—a 70% growth bombshell meant to silence AI bubble critics and ‘circular financing’ doomsayers
events.summary: Nvidia jolted investors on Wednesday with a projection that its revenue would skyrocket by 70% next fiscal year and said demand for its AI chips is growing at 100%, prompting an after-hours stock rally. The 70% preliminary expectation wildly exceeded projections for fiscal 2028 revenue of roughly $570 billion, or 44% growth from fiscal 2027 (the current year). Nvidia’s projected growth, applied to fiscal 2027 revenue and expected revenue, would imply fiscal 2028 revenue in the range of $690 billion to $700 billion, more than $100 billion over the $570 billion analysts had been modeling. “We wanted to make sure that everybody has the same set of information,” CEO Jensen Huang said on a conference call Wednesday. “We’ve got a huge year coming up next year, and it’s going to be pretty extraordinary.” “It is the case that we’ve never forecasted, never guided to a year in advance,” Huang noted later in the call. Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha research at S&P Global, said the magnitude of growth on the top line “blew away expectations” especially given that Nvidia doesn’t normally provide such guidance. “I think what wowed the market was that 70% fiscal year 2028 number that they gave that was way ahead of Visible Alpha consensus,” said Otto. “I think the whole market was like, ‘Whoa, 70%.’” Chief financial officer Colette Kress said customers’ forecasts pointed to Nvidia’s growth doubling next year. She delivered the news to investors after the market closed and her comments sent Nvidia’s stock rallying more than 4% in after-hours trading. However, Nvidia is also battling with significant supply constraints, much like all the other mega-cap tech companies. “Our entire supply chain is challenged, and it’s everybody; everybody is really running flat out,” Huang said. Huang said that if not for these constraints, revenue growth next year would be even greater. “Even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%,” Huang said in response to an analyst question. The never-before-seen growth forecast came after the company disclosed quarterly earnings results that crushed across the board. Revenue for Q2 came in at $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago and sailing past projections of $92.2 billion from analysts. The company earned $2.22 per share on a non-GAAP basis, above the $2.06 to $2.09 expected. Kress guided next quarter to $108 billion in revenue, matching the so-called buyside whisper range of $105 billion to $108 billion.  Nvidia Huang said massive demand was coming from both hyperscale cloud providers as well as non-hyperscalers including sovereign AI, neoclouds, AI startups, and enterprises. The non-hyperscale crowd “represents about half our business, and that’s growing 100% a year,” said Huang. Much of rising demand reflects a shift in the way AI systems are consuming AI compute, particularly as the use of agentic AI becomes more widespread, Huang explained. The amount of compute an AI agent gobbles up versus a human user is about 15 to 100 times greater, depending on the type of task or problem being solved, he said. And the number of agents within businesses is only going to grow. “We have 40,000 employees, roughly,” he said. “In the future, we’ll have 400,000 agents, 4 million agents, and those agents are running continuously.”  ‘We see it differently’ While the booming demand for AI chips has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company, with a market cap of more than $5 trillion, critics have warned about the company’s spate of investments in other companies within the AI industry, from data center operators to frontier model makers like Anthropic. Many view the deals, which Nvidia is financing from its massive cash pile, as creating dangerous interdependencies with the AI business. Kress offered up a defense against critics during the call: “We recognize the scale of this support, and we know some will call this circular financing,” the Nvidia finance chief said. “We see it differently.” She said the frontier AI labs have proven technology leaders, traction from customers, and “skyrocketing” usage.  “We expect them to become the largest technology companies in history,” said Kress. Their growth “isn’t limited by their technology or customer demand. It’s limited by compute.” Still, Nvidia’s involvement has been critical and substantial and, moreover, has led to a drag on the stock price. The company disclosed maximum gross guarantee exposure of $108.5 billion, which mostly stems from credit support for SB Energy’s Ohio tech campus, which will host Nvidia compute leased to OpenAI. The rest is due to $3.5 billion backing lease obligations for AI cloud partners. Nvidia has also publicized investments of nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs and has partnered with private equity giants Apollo , BlackRock , Blackstone , Goldman Sachs , and KKR to raise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure.  Kress said the investments in partners were low-risk, high-reward for Nvidia. “We believe these investments, measured against the strength of their demand, the business they create for us, the ecosystem they build on Nvidia’s platform, and the equity returns on our invested capital will be excellent, and our risk is limited,” said Kress.  Secondly, Kress said demand from the AI labs will contribute to about a quarter of Nvidia’s business next year. She added that Nvidia’s platform is “fungible and durable” and can be used for other business if a partner alters their forward-looking projections.  For smaller, AI-native cloud providers known as neoclouds, Kress said Nvidia offers a deal structure where Nvidia guarantees it will pay for a minimum portion of a data center’s capacity, which satisfies the banks. In exchange, Nvidia takes a cut of the provider’s rental revenue above that threshold.  “Independent capital still underwrites every deal on its own merits. We’re not making loans,” said Kress. “In this model, we get paid twice—once on the hardware sale, and again through the share of rental revenue.” Markets haven’t exactly loved the circular nature of all of these deals. Bill Birmingham, managing director at Rex Financial, said that when reports surfaced in July that Nvidia was in talks to guarantee as much as $250 billion in capacity for OpenAI in Ohio, the credit-default swap market repriced Nvidia’s five-year risk from 40 basis points to 82 basis points. “The equity shed $250 (billion) in turn,” wrote Birmingham in a pre-earnings note seen by Fortune. “Even though the final number came in at $105B, the market read this as less demand and not less risk.” Margin squeeze One point that was slightly less than sterling was Nvidia’s third-quarter gross margin guidance of 74%, down from 75% it delivered in the second quarter, noted S&P Global’s Otto. events.title: Key witness in Meta trial says terms of settlement insufficient to halt apps’ harms to teenagers
events.summary: Exclusive: Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said outcome ‘is not an all clear to say the product is safe’ Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram in settlement The star witness in the US government’s landmark trial against Meta believes that a multibillion-dollar settlement reached on Wednesday does not go far enough to stop the social media giant’s harms to young users. “The limitations that are in the agreement are the equivalent of saying: ‘Well you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day,’” said whistleblower and ex-Facebook employee Arturo Béjar. “It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.” Dozens of states had sued Meta, alleging that it designed addictive products that led to mental health problems for young people such as disordered eating, depression and suicide. The states and the company reached a wide-ranging settlement agreement on Wednesday that will force Meta to make major changes to its platform, including putting strict limits on how much time teens are able to spend on apps like Instagram and Facebook. Béjar’s testimony formed a key part of the government’s case. The former employee, who worked directly with Mark Zuckerberg, testified the Meta CEO lied about the company’s commitment to child safety and ignored warnings about harmful content. Meta rejected Béjar’s criticism that the settlement was too narrowly focused on time limits, pointing to other requirements such as a default setting for teens to see a non-algorithmic feed when they open their accounts and parental controls with an option to revert teens’ feeds to non-personalized content. Many of the changes that Meta must implement following the agreement involve increased parental oversight of app usage and making pre-existing teen safety settings the default for young users. It also creates a “night mode” and “school mode” that restrict app usage during certain times of the day. Several “social comparison” features such as beauty filters and likes will also be disabled by default. While state attorneys general touted the settlement as a victory and Meta called on other platforms to institute similar policies, Béjar argues the settlement lacks independent oversight and does not necessarily make Meta’s platforms safer for young people. Béjar says algorithmic design choices that make Facebook and Instagram addictive and harmful remain unchanged by the agreement and its time limits. He had hoped the agreement would have done more to address how social networks’ algorithms steer young users toward content, as well as instituted independent auditing and quantifiable obligations for reducing harm. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives “This is not an all clear to say that the product is safe,” he said. “As with tobacco and opioids, the product continues to be harmful after the settlement. The work needs to continue in order to make sure that it’s safe enough for young people.” Meta’s spokesperson argued the platform already has extensive protections for teens that guard them from seeing harmful content or engaging in conversations with adults they don’t know. “We have a huge raft of built-in protections,” a Meta spokesperson said. “Béjar’s comments really ignore that and they also ignore the huge value that teens get from social media in all kinds of ways.” A former Facebook safety engineer, Béjar testified for two days during the trial about his view that Meta had adopted a “don’t ask, don’t tell” policy about the safety of children on its platforms. Meta did not accept any wrongdoing in its settlement and denied all allegations during the trial. The company has been facing an avalanche of litigation this year related to claims that it knowingly created products that hooked young users on its platforms and disregarded harms.

events.title: Changes to Facebook and Instagram are key part of Meta’s $17B settlement with the states over harm to teens
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg chose to settle a landmark lawsuit against his company. Jon Putman/Anadolu via Getty Images Meta has agreed to pay up to US$17 billion over 10 years to settle claims brought by a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general. The states argued that the company deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to hook children into using its apps, misled the public about the harm and improperly collected data from children under 13. The settlement , announced by Meta on Aug. 26, 2026, ended a federal trial that had barely begun in Oakland, California. The potential financial exposure in the case was enormous, and Meta’s stock price took a hit. The states argued that penalties could reach hundreds of billions of dollars. Against that backdrop, and with a $1.4 trillion question mark hanging over its valuation , Meta settled, although the company continues to deny wrongdoing. The settlement still requires approval from Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. As a technology policy and law scholar, I follow with interest the litigation against Meta and other social media companies. The basic contours of this settlement are now public, and I believe they deserve careful attention because of the product design changes it might compel Meta, TikTok and YouTube to make. What the states alleged The Oakland case consolidated lawsuits filed in 2023 by 29 state attorneys general following a nationwide investigation that began in 2021. Similar to prior litigation in Los Angeles and New Mexico , the states alleged that Meta engineered features – for example, infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, likes and appearance-altering filters – to exploit vulnerabilities associated with adolescent development and to maximize engagement. States alleged that Meta’s internal research documented links between Instagram use and harms including depression, anxiety and body-image concerns among young people, while the company publicly minimized or concealed those risks. A third set of claims concerned Meta’s collection of data from children under 13 without parental consent, allegedly in violation of federal children’s privacy law. And the states argued that these practices violated state consumer protection statutes as well. That consumer protection claim is particularly important. For decades, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act has protected platforms from liability for content posted by their users. But the states sued Meta instead over the company’s own product design, business practices and alleged misrepresentations, not user-generated content. In opening arguments, California’s lawyer compressed the theory into four words, noting Meta’s business model was to “hook” users, “hold” them, “harvest” their data and “hide” the harm. And there was already precedent at the state level, in Massachusetts , of courts allowing this kind of claim to proceed. The lawsuit and settlement focused on the design of Meta’s social media platforms and how the platforms need to change to protect teens. One legal battle, several different cases It is important not to conflate the cases. While the federal case in Oakland was settled as part of the agreement with the 47 states , major cases against Meta remain active. In Los Angeles, a separate California state-court case resulted in a jury finding Meta and Google liable for negligently designing their products in ways that contributed to a teen girl’s mental health harms, with damages of $4.2 million against Meta and $1.8 million against Google. Those amounts look modest until multiplied across the thousands of similar individual claims now pending. Meta is appealing that decision. And in New Mexico , the state pursued its own enforcement action, alleging that Meta endangered children and violated state consumer protection law. New Mexico won judgments against Meta totaling more than $900 million, which Meta is also challenging. Neither of those cases was part of the federal trial, so today’s settlement does not resolve them, nor does it create legal precedent. What the settlement actually changes The design changes, such as curbing infinite scroll and autoplay, are the substantive core of the agreement. Subject to court approval, teens under 18 on Instagram and Facebook in participating states will get: a default two-hour daily time limit, cumulative across both apps and across multiple accounts, that only a parent can lift a block on app access between midnight and 6 a.m. and muted notifications during school hours (8 a.m. to 3 p.m.), excepting direct messages usage prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous scrolling the option of a non-algorithmic, nonpersonalized feed the ability to turn off autoplay and for parents to set the default to “off” hidden like counts by default blocks on cosmetic surgery and extreme makeup filters strengthened age-detection systems for under-13 accounts Some of these measures are particularly significant because they change the default experience rather than simply adding another setting that users can choose to activate. This lowers the burden on the user. A safety tool that requires a teenager or parent to find, understand and turn on is fundamentally different from a safety constraint built into the product itself. The agreement addresses the architecture that determines how the product operates. In doing so, it recognizes that Meta shares responsibility for the environment it creates, which is crucial because Meta holds significant power to shape how its products are used. Among other changes, the settlement calls for Meta to mute notifications from Facebook and Instagram to teens during school hours. Drazen Zigic/iStock via Getty Images Why the design terms matter more than the money Even $17 billion, spread across a decade, amounts to only roughly 1% of Meta’s expected revenue over the same period. The company has told investors that the settlement will not change its financial guidance beyond a single quarterly expense. More consequential, for Meta and the public, is the requirement to redesign Facebook and Instagram. However, redesign without serious transparency and accountability can quickly become another form of marketing. Meta has promised safety changes before, including teen accounts and expanded parental controls. Verification of the redesign and its real-world impact over time are key. That is where the settlement is both promising and incomplete. An independent auditor will review Meta’s compliance annually, but only for five years, against a 10-year agreement. And Meta has committed to the strongest behavioral terms, the daily time limit and the overnight block, for just five years. It will extend to 10 with stricter defaults only if YouTube and TikTok sign on. Meta has also committed to establish an independent research foundation. events.title: I went to Dollywood for the first time last summer, and I'm still thinking about it. I can't wait to go back.
events.summary: I visited Dolly Parton's Dollywood last summer. Ron Davis/Getty Images I'm a longtime Disney World fan, but last summer, I visited Dollywood for the first time. The park in Tennessee was cheap, had few crowds, and had great snacks. Dollywood pleasantly surprised me and taught me about Dolly Parton's lasting legacy. Disney World has long been my dream vacation. Since I was a kid, I've loved heading down to Florida and spending time in the parks, jumping on some of my favorite rides like "Soarin'" and " Pirates of the Caribbean ." Last summer, I decided to switch it up. I've heard great things about Dollywood in Tennessee , but I was unsure if it would be worth the trip. After talking with a few friends, we decided to bite the bullet and book the trip. I was pleasantly surprised and learned a lot about Dolly Parton herself. A year later, I'm still dreaming about my day in the park, and now with Dolly's passing, I'm eager to get back to the place that celebrates the musical legend. I've long been a fan of her music, so I was excited when the grand entrance welcomed me into the Dolly-verse. The entrance to Dollywood. Frank Olito/Business Insider The buildings at the front of the park housed theaters, shops, and restaurants. It was my first indication that Dollywood was about to transport me into the icon's world. I was impressed by the cheap ticket prices. Purchasing tickets was surprisingly cheap. Frank Olito/Business Insider Before I even arrived in Tennessee, I realized the biggest difference between Dollywood and Disney: the price. I'm used to spending $150 or more for a ticket to Disney World. For this trip, I paid just $99 for admission to two parks — Dollywood and Splash Country . It was well worth it. My first stop at the park was the Dolly Experience: Songteller, a museum about the singer's life. The entrance to Dollywood's museum. Frank Olito/Business Insider Walking through a museum while at an amusement park was a new experience, but it set the tone for the rest of the day. This wasn't an amusement park set around an IP of movies and TV shows. It was a place to celebrate Dolly Parton's life . I remember this museum the most a year later because it taught me just how influential the singer really was. Exploring an amusement park dedicated to a single celebrity was unique and fun. Inside the Dollywood Experience. Frank Olito/Business Insider Dollywood is focused on Dolly Parton — her childhood, her music, and her other achievements. This helped the park feel cohesive and completely immersive. From the moment you enter the park, you explore different parts of Dolly's life. I entered replicas of her childhood home and schoolhouse. The whole park is a celebration of her hometown: the Smoky Mountain region . I wasn't expecting much from the rides at Dollywood, but there was plenty to do. There were plenty of roller coasters. Frank Olito/Business Insider As someone who hates  roller coasters , I was always hesitant when I saw the list of rides at Dollywood. There were a lot of roller coasters, and I am decidedly not a thrill seeker. Even though I only went on a few rides, they were comparable to some of my favorites at other theme parks. Plus, there were plenty of shows to keep me busy throughout the day. Dollywood's cinnamon bread changed me. The cinnamon bread at Dollywood. Frank Olito/Business Insider Disney's frozen treat, Dole Whip , is iconic, and I certainly missed it while in Tennessee, but Dollywood arguably had something better: cinnamon bread. Throughout the park, you could smell the warm scent of cinnamon all day long. When I finally got my hands on a loaf, I instantly melted. The fluffy dough was the perfect treat in the middle of the day. Dollywood wasn't as crowded as I expected. There weren't many crowds. Frank Olito/Business Insider Thankfully, Dollywood wasn't impossible to maneuver. Even though it was July, the park was not packed, so I felt more relaxed. It was easy to move around. Lines for rides were manageable, too; none of them exceeded 45 minutes. That meant I got to immerse myself in all aspects of the park and learn more about the musician. Pigeon Forge also had so much to offer. The pool at Margaritaville Island. Frank Olito/Business Insider Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, is a tourist town, and I loved visiting. It's filled with every activity you can imagine: mini golf, go-karting, dinner shows, shopping, carnivals, and world-class restaurants. I stayed on Margaritaville Island in Pigeon Forge and loved being close to the stores and restaurants. The view of the Ferris wheel from the hotel pool was also great. My first visit to Dollywood far exceeded my expectations. Dollywood. Frank Olito/Business Insider I didn't know what to expect when I first booked my trip to Dollywood, but I was pleasantly surprised at every turn. Dollywood was a great vacation spot because of its rides, immersive theme, and food. It's also the perfect place to celebrate the life of Dolly Parton — something I'm hopeful to do again in the future. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Viral AI startup Instinct has raised $350M at a $2.5B valuation
events.summary: Instinct, a startup founded only last year and helmed by a 23-year-old, has managed to ride the wave of AI enthusiasm toward a gargantuan valuation over the course of the summer. The company, which offers an AI assistant that has inspired enthusiasm among its early users, told the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday that it had raised $250 million in a recent Series B funding round. That new round brings the company’s total funding to $350 million and gives the startup a valuation of $2.5 billion. That new funding round was co-led by Index Ventures and Benchmark, the Journal reported. Instinct, which is offered by the company Spear Street Technology and is led by founder Noah Shinn, is an agent that the company says can efficiently organize your life. Users connect it to their apps and devices and can communicate with it via texts and calls. “I’m thrilled with everything our early users are doing with Instinct,” Shinn wrote in a tweet on Wednesday. “They’ve told us they’ve planned cross-country road trips, bought weekly groceries and concert tickets, and cancelled hundreds of dollars of subscriptions. Someone’s even planning their wedding with Instinct.” Instinct, which rocks a decidedly lo-fi website , is currently in private beta, but it has already inspired a certain amount of controversy due to privacy concerns . events.title: Inside India newsletter: U.S., Russia vie for a bigger slice of the world’s third-largest energy market
events.summary: Monday - Friday, 11:00 - 12:00 SIN/HK | 0500 - 06:00 CET Since the start of the Iran war, Russia has emerged as the largest crude supplier to India while the U.S. has become the top LNG and LPG supplier. Both the U.S. and Russia are looking to expand their trade with India. The U.S. is pushing New Delhi to buy crude from Venezuela to reduce India's dependence on Russian oil. Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India's growing energy requirements are becoming fertile grounds for a contest between the U.S. and Russia, as the two geopolitical rivals seek a bigger share of the world's third-largest energy market. This week I spoke to energy experts to understand how the Iran war, trade deals and tariffs are reshaping India's energy sourcing mix. Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. India is becoming a prime market for the U.S. and Russia, as the two adversaries seek to gain a larger wallet share of the world's third-largest energy consumer . The South Asian country is the world's third-largest importer of crude, fourth-largest buyer of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, and the second-largest importer of liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG. While Russia wants India to continue buying its crude, despite mounting pressure of harsher U.S. tariffs, Washington has been pushing New Delhi to purchase Venezuelan oil to replace Russian barrels. Experts told CNBC that replacing Russian crude at a time when supply from the Middle East is constrained would be "challenging" for New Delhi, even as the country ramps up purchases of Venezuelan crude. "If U.S. and Venezuelan crude are combined, the Americas are becoming more important to India's crude basket," Sumit Ritolia, lead research analyst at market intelligence firm Kpler, told CNBC. Indian refiners cannot replace Russian or Middle Eastern barrels with U.S. crude as it is of a "relatively light" variety, while several Indian refineries are configured to process medium and heavier crude, he said. The "heavier" quality Venezuelan crude solves that problem. India's Venezuelan crude imports have risen from zero in March to 383,000 barrels per day so far in August, according to Kpler data. Together with U.S. crude imports, the two sources accounted for about 11% of India's crude imports over that period. On Monday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that " Russia is expanding its exports [to India] and is ready to continue doing so," hinting at Moscow's increasing share of crude supplies to New Delhi. It is now India's largest crude supplier, accounting for more than 50% of the country's oil imports in June and July and nearly 43% in August so far, according to Kpler data. Between April and July, Russian exports to India rose nearly 60% from last year, according to India's latest trade data. But Moscow isn't the only one gaining a larger share of India's energy market. The U.S. has become India's top supplier of LPG, which is used as a primary cooking fuel in the country, as well as for LNG, which has industrial applications. In July, over 70% of India's LPG imports and nearly a third of LNG supplies originated from the U.S, as per Kpler data. The U.S. energy supplies to India have been "unmatched," Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, said at an event in New Delhi on Saturday, adding that Washington's LPG and LNG supplies to India had risen over 60% over last year. "The Middle East — particularly Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia — traditionally dominated India's LPG imports due to its logistical advantage," said Pankaj Srivastava, senior vice president of commodity markets-oil at Rystad Energy. The Iran war has scuttled that advantage. Since the start of the war, the U.S. has emerged as a leading supplier "supported by bilateral energy agreements, higher US production and constraints on Middle Eastern supply," Srivastava said. But the U.S. also wants a bigger share of India's crude basket. Over the last 12 months, it has used both tariff threats and the promise of a lucrative trade deal to build pressure on India to cut back its Russian crude imports. In August last year, Washington imposed 25% tariff on imports from India as a penalty for buying Russian oil, only to revoke them in February this year. U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. had agreed to cut tariffs against India to 18% after India had "agreed to stop buying Russian Oil, and to buy much more from the United States and, potentially, Venezuela." India, however, has not endorsed the details shared by Trump and maintains that ensuring energy security is the sole driver of its energy purchases. Steep tariffs could make a comeback as the Russia Sanctions bill that proposes up to a 100% levy on countries buying Russian energy supplies will move to the U.S. House for final approval in September.

events.title: Prudential sees new business profit growth slow, announces US$300m share buy-back
events.summary: New business profit increases 8 per cent to US$1.38 billion in first half as market braces for potential fall in number of mainland visitors British insurer Prudential announced a US$300 million share buy-back, to be completed by December, as it reported an 8 per cent increase in new business profit for the first half of the year. The buy-back and slower profit growth came amid market concerns over a potential pullback in mainland Chinese visitors to Hong Kong that could test the performance of insurers in one of their largest markets. New business profit – a key metric tracking the future profitability of newly written life insurance policies – rose to US$1.38 billion in the six months ended June 30, the company said on Thursday. That matched analysts’ estimates. The financial results showed a lower growth rate than in the first half of 2025, when new business profit surged 12 per cent to US$1.26 billion. In the first half of this year, adjusted operating profit increased by 9 per cent to US$1.81 billion, or 58.4 US cents per share. Annual premium equivalent sales – a major sales indicator combining regular and single premiums – rose 3 per cent to US$3.42 billion, up from US$3.29 billion recorded in the same period last year.

events.title: El-Sayed says ‘no plans’ to campaign with Piker
events.summary: The News FARMINGTON HILLS, MICH. — Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed put more distance between himself and Hasan Piker on Wednesday night, telling Semafor in an interview that he has “no plans” to campaign with the controversial streamer. El-Sayed has taken heat from some in his party over his associations with Piker , the left-wing streamer whose comments about American Jews have faced intense criticism in recent days. Democrats pushed for El-Sayed to more directly condemn Piker and his comments, though El-Sayed framed the whole episode as a nonissue in the election. “Most people are a lot more worried about things like, what are you going to do about my groceries? What are you going to do about my healthcare? What are you going to do about the fact that I cannot afford [to enroll] my kid in baseball, even though my kid’s a really great baseball player?” El-Sayed said at a banquet hall in the Detroit suburbs. “Those are the things I’m talking about, and the effort to make this race about a streamer in LA is actually kind of laughable.” He said he hasn’t talked to Senate Democratic leadership or the caucus’ campaign arm about Piker. But his record of publicly interacting with Piker — including at a pool party just before the primary — remains a sore point among some Michigan Democrats. Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten, who’d backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, has signaled she won’t yet endorse El-Sayed over his links to Piker, whom she’s said is endangering Democrats’ chances of winning a majority. And the brouhaha over Piker’s singling out of Democratic House candidate Jeremy Moss on his livestream discouraged Moss from endorsing El-Sayed. The back-and-forth over Piker has irked other Michigan Democrats, who see it as a sideshow distracting from their efforts to hold outgoing Sen. Gary Peters’ seat and flip several House districts. At an earlier El-Sayed event in Ann Arbor, Rep. Debbie Dingell vented her frustrations onstage: “Don’t any reporter ask me again about Hasan Piker,” she said, calling the controversey a move by Republicans to divide Democrats. “Is the reason he exercises and looks buff why he has so many followers?” she quipped. “Perhaps it’s because I’ve been fighting for progressive values that many Americans identify with for over a decade and many recognize it despite the manufactured outrage from reactionary media outlets?” Piker replied . Meanwhile, Republicans have reveled in the Democratic divides, with the GOP Senate nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, and the state party knocking El-Sayed for his associations with Piker. “Conman Abdul El-Sayed still refuses to name and condemn his campaign spokesman, Hasan Piker, for the vile antisemitic rhetoric numerous Democrats across the country are finally denouncing,” Michigan Republican Party spokesperson Greg Manz said in a statement. El-Sayed dismissed a potential fundraising gap in the race, which could occur if donors were pushed towards Rogers or if outside groups like AIPAC intervened on Rogers’ behalf. “I’m not particularly worried about how much money the super PACs and the corporate PACs and AIPAC are going to spend to try and support him,” he said. “I’m a lot more focused on conversations I want to have with Michigan voters about the contrast between us.” Notable El-Sayed is still in conversations with Moss, who also said he won’t support Rogers, the Detroit News reported . In an appearance on Semafor’s in the wake of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s win, Piker expressed dismay at being invoked in intra-Democratic debates. “I should never be the conversation,” he told Ben Smith and Max Tani.

events.title: Fed Gov Lisa Cook’s lawyer fires back at Trump's renewed threat to oust her
events.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook pushed back on President Donald Trump's revived effort to remove her from the central bank. Allegations of mortgage fraud lodged against Cook by the Trump administration "remain unfounded and untrue," attorney Abbe Lowell wrote. Lowell noted that Trump and others in his administration, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Attorney General Todd Blanche, have been accused of similar conduct. A lawyer for Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Wednesday pushed back on President Donald Trump 's revived effort to remove her from the central bank, telling the White House in a five-page letter that allegations of mortgage fraud against her "remain unfounded and untrue." Lawyer Abbe Lowell's defense of Cook came just before the deadline for a reply that Trump aide Dan Scavino set three weeks earlier, when he wrote to Cook that there is "sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements." Trump, who wants the Fed to sharply lower interest rates, first moved to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden , in late August 2025. He took that step after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte sent a criminal referral to the Department of Justice accusing Cook of possible mortgage fraud, alleging she claimed two different properties as her primary residence at the same time. Cook denied the allegations and filed a lawsuit challenging her dismissal. The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump from firing Cook, but left the president with a path to try again to remove her. Lowell, in his letter to White House counsel David Warrington, said that trying to fire Cook based on Pulte's referral "would ignore the facts and the law." Scavino's Aug. 5 letter to Cook describes "two acts by Governor Cook that, 'taken together,' supposedly constitute grounds for her removal," Lowell wrote. "But neither of those acts shows intentional wrongdoing or amounts to a crime, and neither constitutes 'cause' under the Federal Reserve Act." Canada unveils retaliatory tariffs on about $20B of U.S. goods Trump targets Iran's trade lifelines — here are the countries most exposed Mark Walter's TWG Global hires Goldman vet Markowitz as top lawyer amid probe Trump oil and gas stocks gained up to $15.5 million, Democrats say Trump admin unveils anti-Iran global sanctions plan, signals China not exempt Lowell also noted that Trump himself, along with others in his administration including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Attorney General Todd Blanche, have reportedly also listed multiple properties as primary residences in the past. "An inadvertent oversight is not fraudulent or criminal," Lowell wrote. "Governor Cook's apparent mistake on a form provided to her by her lender, which was aware of her other residences, was unintentional, not criminal, and occurred in her private capacity before she took office." Attempting to fire Cook on the basis of Pulte's allegations would be selective, Lowell added, and "would raise troubling questions about why President Trump is singling out Governor Cook." The letter also included a declaration in Cook's defense from Suffolk University Law School research law professor Kathleen Engel. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.

events.title: Bookstores struggle to fill shelves after cyber attack on major publisher
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cyber attack targeting Hachette Australia subsidiary hurts bookshops and authors Melbourne bookshop owner Jaye Chin-Dusting is concerned about stock supply leading up to the busy Christmas period. ( ABC News: Ethan White ) Independent bookstores are struggling to meet customer demands after one of Australia's largest book distributors experienced a cyber attack six weeks ago. The cyber attack against Alliance Distribution Services (ADS) has left Australian authors unable to provide sufficient stock for events. Hachette Australia, which owns ADS, says restoring full operations securely remains its top priority. A cyber attack on one of the country's major publishing distributors has left bookshops and authors struggling to fill their shelves in the lead-up to their busiest trading period. Hachette Australia said unauthorised activity on the computer systems of its distribution subsidiary, Alliance Distribution Services (ADS), was believed to have occurred on July 18. The incident has severely disrupted the distribution of titles by Hachette's authors across Australia, with independent bookstores unable to fill shelves as they prepare to order stock leading up to its high-demand Christmas period. Jaye Chin-Dusting, who is owner of Mary Martin Bookshop in Melbourne, first noticed there was a problem when books published by Hachette stopped arriving. Jaye Chin-Dusting says new release titles have been prioritised by ADS, but supply of books already released remains limited. ( ABC News: Ethan White ) "ADS would supply us 15 to 20 per cent of the books that we usually have on our shelves," she said. "In the first couple of weeks, I think we weren't really sure what was going on. "Certainly, books weren't arriving." Children's author Danielle Binks's plans to travel to Adelaide next month to visit schools and launch her new book, Shakespeare in the Orchard, have been thrown in doubt. "Normally when I do any interstate visits, I'll pop into bookstores and sign copies of my book," said the Melbourne author, who publishes titles with Hachette. "I've been told I can't for this September trip, obviously because Hachette has no way of knowing who has stock and can't supply them with more at the moment." Danielle Binks says a planned trip to Adelaide, including presentations to school students, is in doubt without a guaranteed supply of copies of her new book. ( Supplied ) Binks said the incident had affected the entire Australian publishing industry. "My publicists and sales team at Hachette are equally gutted that they can't do their jobs to their full extent," she said. The incident was brought to wider attention by Melbourne author Maxine Beneba Clarke, who took to social media last week sharing her experience. "For me, this will mean the loss of a large part of my income, possibly for years, and the loss of thousands of young authors," she wrote on Instagram last week. Melbourne writer Maxine Beneba Clarke brought the cyber attack to public attention. ( ABC Arts: Leah Jing McIntosh ) In a statement, Hachette Australia told the ABC it was continuing to restore systems and services, following "unauthorised activity" in ADS computer systems. "We know this has been frustrating for our authors, booksellers, readers and people, and we are sorry for the impact it has had," a spokesperson said. Hachette, who owns Alliance Distribution Services, says it is working to ensure commitments around events are delivered where possible. ( Supplied: Alliance Distribution Services ) The company said while progress was being made, it was not yet in a position to confirm a timeline for a full return to normal operations. "Restoring full operations securely remains our top priority, and we are grateful for the patience and support of everyone across the industry while we work through this." Ms Chin-Dusting said it had been six weeks since supply issues began, slowing down the quantity of stock her business was able to purchase. "ADS has been pretty good at nevertheless manually pushing out the new releases. So it's the backlists — books that have been out for a little bit — that are more difficult to get," she explained. Jaye Chin-Dusting says major book retailers can afford alternative options, leaving smaller independent stores like her own vulnerable. ( ABC News: Ethan White ) Ms Chin-Dusting said in the meantime, Hachette has suggested booksellers source stock through other means, including purchasing them from the online retailer Booktopia or international suppliers. "Of course, that then increases the cost of the book because of the freight that comes through.

events.title: The toy industry's latest craze is cheap, colorful and very squishy
events.summary: U.S. squishy toy sales quadrupled year-over-year to about $297 million in January through June. Social media has played a key role in fueling the squishy toy craze. The squishy toy craze is also reaching Southeast Asian markets. Dumplings, ice cubes and gummy bears — squishable ones, anyway — are some of the hottest toys of 2026 Squishy toys have been around for years, but products such as NeeDoh, made by Massachusetts-based Schylling, have exploded in popularity this year, helped by their relatively low prices and social media appeal. U.S. sales of squishy toys reached about $297 million through June, quadrupling from a year earlier, Kristen McLean, vice president of client insights and the leader of market-research firm Circana's Entertainment Knowledge Group, told CNBC. Unit sales jumped nearly 200% to 58.6 million over the same period, according to McLean. "While the price and the stores they are selling in make them widely available and accessible from a price perspective, the NeeDoh run in particular started on social media," McLean said. The combination of "fun colors, interesting packaging, stress relief and play" helped lay the viral foundation for broader adoption, she said. "They really managed to capture a moment in the zeitgeist." TikTok Shop has grown to represent 1% of total retail sales and 3% of e-commerce sales in just two years, according to Circana's Social Commerce Tracking data, with toys, hobbies and collectibles ranking as the third-largest category on the platform. Their relatively low prices could also make it easier for online attention to translate into purchases. "Squishy toys are widely accessible and relatively inexpensive, making them an easy impulse purchase after consumers see them trending on social media," said Loo Wee Teck, global insight manager for toys and games at market intelligence company Euromonitor International. "Against a backdrop of economic uncertainty, rising stress and digital fatigue, consumers are increasingly drawn to products that offer simple moments of comfort and relaxation," Loo said. Kevin Kwok, director of Kids Village Asia, the sole distributor of Schylling's NeeDoh in Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei, told CNBC that inbound trade and retailer inquiries have risen nearly 20-fold from the same period last year. "The shift in demand has been dramatic," Kwok said. He said the surge took off around January, driven largely by social media, including celebrities showcasing NeeDoh on their platforms. "What makes the current boom different is that squishy toys are increasingly valued for their sensory and emotional benefits, not just as novelty items," Loo added. NeeDoh didn't respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Circana's Checkout Toys Recipient Data for the three months ended June showed that 60% of NeeDoh purchasers were parents buying for their children, while 18.2% reported buying the toys for themselves. Children aged 7 to 12 were the largest group of recipients for both genders, and 72% of all recipients were female. After the massive sales surge in such a short time, the question is how long the squishy boom can continue. "The current hype will fade over time, like fidget spinners, but the broader appeal of sensory and tactile play will persist," Euromonitor's Loo said. "As consumers increasingly seek simple ways to relax and disconnect from digital overload, toys that support mindful play will remain relevant."

events.title: U.S. still watching allies for alignment of interests even amid defense pullback, analyst says
events.summary: The U.S. has announced that it will cancel joint marine drills with South Korea due to Iran war constraints. Washington wants its allies to spend more on defense while it retains influence over which partnerships are preferable. Asian countries are looking for ways to increase defense spending and forge new security ties as Washington steps back. A U.S. pullback from Asia will give regional allies more responsibility for their own defense — but Washington is still watching for alignment with its own interests, according to Derek Grossman, professor of political science at the University of Southern California. "The guiding mantra has been less of the U.S. is more, so long as countries who are doing things in the absence of the United States are doing things in line with what the U.S. wants," Grossman told "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday. Grossman's comments came after President Donald Trump reiterated calls to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, citing the cost of drills, Seoul's refusal to support U.S. war efforts against Iran, and his "good" relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. This week, the U.S. military also moved to cancel joint marine drills with South Korea that were scheduled for next month, due to constraints from the Iran war. Washington appears willing to accept more regional cooperation without direct American involvement - as long as those partnerships remain aligned with U.S. interests, Grossman said.. "If Australia, the Philippines and Japan are meeting up without the United States in their own 'minilateral' security grouping, that's fine because we trust all three of those countries," he said. "The problem is when Japan starts meeting up with China and Russia," he added. Allies will likely respond by increasing "their military spending, investing more heavily in their own defense, and forming new partnerships with neighbors," said Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis from Defense Priorities. "Over time, regional partnerships that do not include the United States can provide U.S. allies with a Plan B." Grossman said that the focus of the current administration has been the defense of Taiwan, even as the U.S. "systematically deprioritizes other areas of Asia." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that "no one is contemplating walking away from Taiwan," reaffirming Washington's commitment to its security while en route to Asia last year. He also warned Beijing against "destabilizing actions" on Taiwan ahead of Trump's meeting with Xi in May this year. Still, Grossman said it remains to be seen how effective that stance is. "The question immediately posed should be: how can you defend Taiwan when you're fighting a war in Iran and wasting munitions there?" he said. "I don't think the United States has really answered that question sufficiently."

events.title: Amazon just tripled its order of Nvidia chips over ‘surging demand’
events.summary: Amazon and Nvidia just got a lot closer. The two companies announced Wednesday an expanded partnership that includes a deal to add another 2 million Nvidia GPU chips to Amazon’s data centers. These GPUs, which are designed to handle the heavy compute demands of training and running AI models, include Nvidia Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra GPUs. The chips will head to Amazon Web Services’ data centers in 2027 and 2028. The announcement, made during Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call, comes just five months after Amazon agreed to deploy more than 1 million Nvidia GPUs across AWS infrastructure starting this year. Nvidia said in a statement that since then, “demand has exceeded those expectations.” Neither company shared financial terms. It’s unclear what the exact return will be for Nvidia. But considering GPU unit costs, the deal is worth tens of billions of dollars. The announcement is notable not just because of its size and the speed in which it grew, but also because it extends beyond Amazon buying more Nvidia chips. And it’s happening even as Amazon invests in its own potentially competing AI chips. Nvidia said Wednesday that its technology, including the networking hardware that connects thousands of GPUs into one system, as well as its open models, CPUs, data processing software, and robotics platform, will also be integrated across AWS. The companies said “surging demand” from startups, enterprises, AI labs, and even governments influenced the decision to work more closely. The expanded partnership comes as Amazon ramps up its own AI chip efforts — particularly with CPUs, which are the general-purpose processors at the heart of servers. Amazon has been building its own chips to lessen its dependence on Nvidia and even compete with the chip giant. Amazon’s AI chief, Peter DeSantis, has said that AWS is in talks to sell its Trainium chips — which are a direct alternative to Nvidia’s H100 or Blackwell chips for deep learning workloads — to other companies for use in data centers. Amazon’s Arm-built Graviton CPU is also seen as a challenger to traditional server chips from Intel and AMD. Amazon has said its custom chip business is growing, noting on its last earnings call that it crossed a $25 billion annualized revenue run rate, driven by $225 billion in total commitments from AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. But it seems Nvidia is still the GOAT in the world of AI chips. With the 2 million GPU chips Amazon is adding to AWS starting in the third quarter, Nvidia also plans to send an unspecified number of Vera CPUs, “some integrated with Rubin, others standalone,” according to Nvidia CFO Colette Kress. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has big plans for the company’s Vera CPUs, boasting back in May that he had found a “brand-new $200 billion TAM” for the company. Aside from AWS, Kress said Wednesday that Nvidia expects Vera to be deployed by “every major hyperscaler, neocloud, AI lab, and system OEM, with shipments already underway to our lead partners,” which include Oracle and SpaceXAI. The partnership is also extending to Amazon’s warehouse robots and enterprise offerings. Kress said Amazon plans to adopt Nvidia’s full physical AI stack to power its fleet of robots. The stack includes Omniverse (its simulation and digital twin platform); Cosmos (its world model platform); Isaac (its robotics development platform); and Jetson (computing hardware for robots and edge AI). This week, Nvidia also introduced a new version of Jetson , designed as a more accessible robotics computer for “entry-level edge AI.” On the enterprise side, AWS will serve Nvidia’s Nemotron family of open models on Amazon Bedrock, its managed foundation model platform, and SageMaker, its managed cloud service. Nvidia also reported Wednesday that it recorded sales of $96.2 billion for the second quarter, beating analyst estimates. Data center revenue made up the majority of Nvidia’s sales for the quarter at $89 billion, up 117% from a year ago. Nvidia said it expects revenue to reach $108 billion in the third quarter, some of which will come from its next-gen Rubin GPUs. Nvidia said it began production shipments this quarter. Investors have been looking out for Rubin’s initial Q3 sales for signs that demand will continue into Nvidia’s next generation of hardware. Nvidia has committed $279 billion to secure supply and manufacturing capacity for current and future data-center projects, up substantially from $119 billion last quarter, as the chipmaker looks to secure memory and manufacturing capacity to meet AI demand over the next few years. That commitment includes $92 billion in projected spending for the rest of the fiscal year and another $87 billion in fiscal year 2028. “The thing that matters for the industry is that AI is now doing productive and useful work,” Huang said during Wednesday’s call.

events.title: Fed governor Lisa Cook: "No legitimate basis for removal" on Trump mortgage claims
events.summary: Lawyers for Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook have submitted their case for why she cannot legally be fired, as President Trump seeks new avenues for dismissing the Biden appointee for cause. The big picture: After the Supreme Court ruled against Trump's attempt to fire Cook last year over allegations that she claimed two different properties as her primary residence in mortgage documents, the White House has sought to introduce a more formal process in pursuit of the same goal. It is a closely watched case that may determine the political independence of America's central bank, by setting how high the bar is for a president to fire Fed governors. Driving the news: Three weeks ago, the White House asked for her response to the substance of those allegations, which her lawyers submitted — and distributed to reporters — Wednesday evening. Cook's lawyers argue that "there is no legitimate basis for" removing Cook from the Fed board, where her term extends to 2034, and that the purported errors were "an entirely inadvertent oversight." They say that she was fully transparent with her lender and note media reports that Trump himself and five members of his cabinet have also had dubious claims of primary residency on a property in the past. Catch up quick: Trump announced that he was firing Cook about a year ago for cause, alleging mortgage fraud after housing finance regulator Bill Pulte showed she had mortgage applications for two separate properties as a primary residence in a short time frame. The Federal Reserve Act gives governors of the central bank 14-year terms to insulate them from politics, but says the president can remove them "for cause." The Supreme Court ruled that Cook could stay in her job while the attempted firing is adjudicated, but did not lay out precise criteria of what clears the bar of firing a Fed governor for cause or how a president must establish it. In an apparent effort to establish legal cause, White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino wrote to Cook earlier this month citing the apparent mortgage application errors and asking for her defense. What they're saying: "The process for seeking financing for the Atlanta condominium… began with Governor Cook using the lender's website to seek information about a 'vacation home' mortgage — a clear indication of the loan type she was looking to acquire," wrote Abbe David Lowell, Cook's attorney. "The lender, which previously worked with Governor Cook to refinance her Massachusetts property earlier that year, knew that she had lived in Michigan for more than 15 years and worked full-time as a tenured professor at Michigan State University. Governor Cook gave no indication that she was leaving to take any new job in Atlanta," Lowell wrote. Other documents how that Cook "regularly indicated her 'primary residence' or 'permanent residence' to be Michigan" and she "confirmed that her Atlanta property was a '2nd Home.'" "Governor Cook's actions demonstrate that there was no intentional misconduct and zero intent to defraud or mislead." Of note: Lowell cites media reports of Trump himself and several cabinet members making dubious claims of a property's primary residence status, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The other side: The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. What's next: The question now is whether Trump again attempts to fire Cook, with more of a review process — and if so, how the courts respond.

events.title: US diesel supplies hit record low as demand season looms
events.summary: Retail diesel prices in the US are already above US$5.60 a gallon, near the highest they have been since the beginning of the US-Iran war. US supplies of diesel have fallen to the lowest seasonal level ever, threatening to push prices even higher for the global economy’s workhorse fuel just as heating and agricultural seasons kick into gear. Stocks of distillate fuel oil – a category of fuels that most prominently includes diesel – stood at 103.4 million barrels in the week ending Aug 21, according to data released on Aug 26 by the Energy Information Administration. Stockpiles have never been that low at this time of year, according to data stretching back to the early 1980s. Global diesel demand typically crests around October as the beginning of winter heating season and harvests in the Northern Hemisphere meet planting season in the Southern Hemisphere. Increasing demand for the fuel amid precariously low stockpiles could push prices even higher and stoke energy-driven inflation. The war in Iran roiled energy markets, but crude flows have proven more resilient than refined products, with exports of refined fuels through the Strait of Hormuz reduced to almost nothing. Compounding the problem: Russia’s suspension of diesel exports amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. Moscow is considering extending the export ban for another month, squeezing trade partners even further. Retail diesel prices in the US are already above US$5.60 a gallon, near the highest they have been since the beginning of the US-Iran war and fewer than 20 cents off the all-time record set in 2022. Meanwhile, US petrol prices have remained stubbornly above US$4 a gallon. US refiner margins for making diesel have surged to record highs in recent weeks, indicating the outsized global demand for US-produced fuel. US exports of the fuel have touched extraordinarily high levels, but the supplies are far from enough to make up for the balance of lost product. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Republicans are dismissing affordability. That could be a problem in November
events.summary: Republicans are acknowledging the high cost of living but largely downplaying affordability, which CNBC polling has identified as voters' No. 1 concern ahead of the midterm election. President Donald Trump quipped that affordability was "devised" by Democrats, while Vice President JD Vance said groceries "cost what they cost." Separately, Sen. Darline Graham, after winning the GOP nomination for a full term, followed up a condemnation of Democratic support for universal healthcare by saying her parents had to work while they were sick and died young. Voters are worried about the cost of living . Comments from the GOP this week are not likely to console them. President Donald Trump , in an interview Wednesday, said the word "affordability" was "devised" by Democrats to disparage him. The Republican National Committee sent out a fundraising text attributed to Vice President JD Vance that said groceries "cost what they cost." And Sen. Darline Graham , R-S.C., who won the nomination for a full Senate term on Tuesday, disparaged federally run universal healthcare before recalling with nostalgia her parents heading to work even if they were sick. The set of comments over the past 24 hours exemplifies the challenges ahead for Republicans as they race to save their majorities in Congress in the midterm election , which looms less than 10 weeks away. Democrats are hammering Republicans on the campaign trail over the cost of living, which remains stubbornly high amid the war with Iran. The White House and Republicans also have few levers to pull to remedy affordability concerns immediately. Voters are also loud and clear that affordability is their top concern in this election. Respondents to CNBC's most recent All-America Economic Survey said the cost of food and groceries was voters' top concern, and Democrats held a 7 percentage point lead on handling that issue. Personal consumption expenditures price index data released Wednesday rose .2% from June, leaving the annual inflation rate at 3.7%. The report, released by the Commerce Department, also showed inflation-adjusted consumer spending was flat from the month prior, compared with a .4% gain in June. Political analysts say the comments from top Republicans risk coming across as tone-deaf to voters struggling with high prices. "Republicans are driving the car straight into an affordability wall at full throttle, and they're yelling that the barrier is just a media hoax," said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center. "Well it's not, it's a barrier, and all the while the tariff policies and the conflicts are actively cutting the brakes." Republicans may learn the same lesson Democrats did in 2024, he told CNBC. "To be fair, the same thing happened in 2024," Paleologos said. "[Joe] Biden's people kept talking about the metrics on the dashboard, bragging to voters about horsepower and top speed when the middle class was riding on flat tires." The Republican National Committee defended the GOP's record in a statement to CNBC. "After inheriting four years of Democrats' failed economy, President Trump and Republicans are delivering the comeback Americans voted for: historic tax relief, lower prescription drug prices, critical support for farmers and rural hospitals, and Trump Accounts to give the next generation a financial head start," said RNC spokesman Max Lippel. "While Democrats' popularity sinks to historic lows, Republicans are putting more money back in families' pockets, rebuilding prosperity, and making the American Dream possible again." Canada unveils retaliatory tariffs on about $20B of U.S. goods Trump targets Iran's trade lifelines — here are the countries most exposed Mark Walter's TWG Global hires Goldman vet Markowitz as top lawyer amid probe Trump oil and gas stocks gained up to $15.5 million, Democrats say Trump admin unveils anti-Iran global sanctions plan, signals China not exempt Trump's comments Wednesday came during an interview with Glenn Beck, a political ally and radio host. Beck asked the president to respond to Americans who believe there is an "affordability crisis." In response, the president said that "affordability is interesting because the Democrats caused affordability," arguing that prices are too high because of former President Joe Biden's administration, which ended more than a year and a half ago. "I inherited high prices, and then from the first day, they started using the word 'affordability,'" Trump said. "It was a new word. Nobody ever heard the word. It was a new word that they devised because they're quite good at that." Kyle Kondik, managing editor of election forecasting newsletter "Sabato's Crystal Ball" at the University of Virginia, said blaming the prior administration is unlikely to work in a midterm year. "I think trying to blame the past administration for the problems of the present is generally a dud of an argument," Kondik said.

events.title: Experts' five tips to make a rented property feel like home
events.summary: It can be a balancing act making a rented property feel like your own. You want somewhere that feels warm and personal but without spending a fortune changing a flat or house owned by someone else and making alterations that put a deposit at risk. Higher average mortgage rates and hefty deposits mean buying a home is out of reach for many, who are renting for longer . The good news is that transforming a rental doesn't have to mean a major renovation. With a free weekend, a relatively small budget and a few clever changes, even a bland or tired-looking place can be spruced-up. We asked B&Q chief executive Graham Bell and interior designers Lara Clarke and Lydia Lloyd for their top tips that won't break the bank or annoy a landlord. Before making anything permanent, check what your tenancy agreement allows. Bell, of DIY chain B&Q, says many landlords may be open to sensible improvements, particularly where something is being upgraded rather than fundamentally changed. But getting permission first avoids an expensive argument when you move out. Bell also says it is important to take time to prepare properly. "The biggest mistake is that people don't plan enough," he says. "It's all the planning that goes into it that's important, making sure you have everything. "My dad would tell me to always measure twice and cut once." He recommends deciding exactly what you want to achieve, measuring the space and buying everything you need before you start. Online tutorials can also help with relatively simple DIY projects. Choose changes you can take with you If you don't want to spend money improving someone else's property, focus on temporary changes that can come with you when you move. Bell recommends renter-friendly products such as stick-on tiles for the kitchen, suction storage products in the bathroom and expandable blinds that can be fitted without drilling. Interior designer Clarke says artwork is probably the easiest way to make a rental feel more homely because it "instantly makes a space feel more occupied and finished". She suggests looking for affordable vintage oil paintings, exhibition posters or framed sketches at antique markets, then securing them with command strips so they can be removed without leaving holes in the plaster. Lighting is one of the quickest ways to transform a space. Bell says rentals often come with "bright, bright lights", but swapping them out for something warmer can dramatically change the atmosphere of a room. He suggests experimenting using lightbulbs or strip lighting with different tones. Strip lighting is often found in kitchens but a softer glow can change the whole feel of the space without requiring a major renovation. Rather than depending on a single overhead light, Clarke recommends building up different sources from around the room. "Mood lighting really helps make a space feel more cosy and homely," she says. "Add table and floor lamps too and there are plenty of battery-powered options around now so you don't have to worry about finding a plug socket." Clarke says the effect can be made even cosier by pairing lighting with soft furnishings, such as floor-to-ceiling curtains and scatter cushions in different colours and patterns. A simple way to make a rented house stop feeling temporary is to create a corner that reflects who you are. Lloyd, a home designer at M&S, says it doesn't need to cost a lot since a "few carefully chosen accessories [can] make a big difference". She says: "Books, framed photographs, decorative objects and houseplants help tell your story and can make even a temporary space feel more personal and lived in." To add a little something extra, Clarke suggests "sourcing characterful pieces". "Avoid flatpack furniture," she says. "And source things from online marketplaces or antique markets for unique pieces that tell a story and make a space feel more lived-in and curated over time." Lloyd believes scent is a "simple but powerful way to make a home feel inviting". Buying candles, diffusers and room sprays "can help create a warm, cosy atmosphere, especially as we move into the colder months". She recommends fragrances such as sandalwood, cedarwood, cinnamon and cardamom as they "are perfect for bringing a sense of comfort into the home". She also suggests "adding layers of texture through cushions, throws and blankets" thinking about mixing materials like velvet, boucle or chunky knits. events.title: Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these skills
events.summary: Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Lynn Bassett, Barbour's HR director, values workers who can build positive relationships within a team The ability to communicate, collaborate and solve problems are among skills that employers say they are looking for in potential job hires. In a major five-year study, the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) identified six key transferable skills that will count as much as qualifications in getting and keeping a job in the coming decade. It comes as NFER research, published last year , external , suggests it may become even harder to find a job as AI and automation could see up to three million low- to mid-level jobs disappearing by 2035. As more than one million young people are not in education, employment or training - the highest level in over a decade - we have been speaking to businesses about how people can demonstrate the key skills employers are looking for. Knowing how to organise, plan and prioritise is key Christian Townsley, co-founder of the North Bar group, says he looks for an ability to keep a "cool head" when conducting trial shifts One of the big shocks for many leaving education and trying to get into work is the sudden lack of structure, so being able to prioritise your own work is seen by many employers as essential. In Leeds, Christian Townsley, the co-founder of the North Bar group, says working in a busy bar is all about staying calm and keeping a "cool head". "It's important that you can organise, you can multitask, you can identify who's next at the bar and remember that," he says. Townsley offers trial shifts as part of the recruitment process, to give job seekers an opportunity to showcase these skills in action. "We'll observe them working with customers, working with the team, seeing how they fit in, seeing how they communicate," he says. As people get promoted, they are expected to take on more responsibilities and be able to manage them within the role. "There's organisation, ordering beer, pricing beer, planning social media, marketing, recruiting," Townsley adds. Problem-solving and decision-making go hand in hand Many employers want new recruits to be able to react to issues as they arise and take decisive action. Maria Aderonmu went from a political science degree to a career at Morgan Sindall Infrastructure, a company that delivers infrastructure projects across energy, defence, rail and more in the UK. Now working in strategy, Aderonmu often has to think on the go and says "adapting to each kind of situation" has been one of the biggest things she's learnt through work. At university, she was involved in the debating society and now realises that has prepared her for thinking on her feet. Maria, who works in the construction industry, says time spent in the debating society at university prepared her for thinking on her feet People director India Chaplin says she doesn't expect "every young person to have come across every scenario". Her tip is to think about how your experiences of solving problems outside of work - at school, say, or when you have been part of a team - could apply to a work setting. "There's lots of different ways that people can show the softer skills that we're looking for and how they would approach a problem, even if it was a scenario they've maybe not come across to help think how they would put that into practice in the working environment." Good communication builds relationships and reduces conflict General manager Jake Readman, from North Bar, says "developing communication skills" is key in a busy bar. It is also important to learn "how to de-escalate and resolve conflict in certain situations", he says. "Be confident in who you are as a person and your ability to learn new skills and rise to new situations," he added, "and also the ability to show a little bit of initiative." El Cousins says she likes to give her CV in person so that employers "get an idea of your personality" As we speak to Readman, El Cousins comes into North Bar to hand in her CV. She says she likes to meet potential employers face to face because "they get an idea of your personality". "I think that matters quite a lot and that doesn't always come across on a piece of paper or online," Cousins tells us. Readman is impressed by Cousins and later offers her some shifts. Collaboration is essential for teamwork At Barbour's factory in South Shields, HR director Lynn Bassett says being able to collaborate is something they look for in everyone they recruit. "Each department is interlinked with one another so working as one team is really important," she says. Bassett says what they are looking for when hiring is how people can talk about their own experiences of collaboration. "They might not have the specific experience that's needed for the role, but we look more at those transferable skills." Addie Pattas has started a placement with Barbour during her fashion degree.
