events.title: Tax on AI tokens could fill UK fiscal slump
events.summary: A UK think tank has proposed an international tax on AI output that would target the tokens it produces to bridge feared gaps in government revenue. The report author, Oxford professor Ben Ansell, argues that, for a variety of reasons – mainly domestic ageing but also the structure of the economy – reform of Britain’s tax system is increasingly unavoidable. The Institute for Public Policy Research, which is close to the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham's leadership team, has said the UK's current tax system has become too skewed in favour of age and wealth. One of the main long-term changes would be to promote an international token tax for jobs lost to AI. “An AI token tax, to directly trap a portion of the value created by AI models,” Prof Ansell writes. “Given that this would require consistent auditing of AI companies, it would likely rely on international co-operation.” Given the political obstacles in Washington and elsewhere to achieving this backing, the report considers other domestic changes. In the short term, the report said equalisation of capital gains tax with marginal rates of income tax would help offset the divide between old and young. It also raises a tax on personal behaviours that are “speculative”, including gambling and crypto investing. These moves could bridge the gap if AI starts to eat into revenue from payroll levies. IPPR's findings would require AI companies to audit their token production process and pay on any resulting revenue. International co-operation would hold the key to a workable tax regime on AI. “If the UK were alone in implementing a token tax, it potentially faces competitiveness issues as high-value service sector AI app users in the UK pay taxes not faced by rival firms abroad,” the IPPR report, out overnight, said. “Moreover, with frontier AI models largely based in the US and China, Britain would face the difficulty of asking foreign companies to engage in continuous auditing for British fiscal needs.” Population ageing will account for almost 80 per cent of the additional fiscal pressure facing the UK by 2075, according to a new paper published by IPPR, which argues Britain needs a new fiscal settlement that shifts taxes away from young people and work and instead towards property as well as older people and wealth. The ageing of the UK population will drive tax changes over the rest of the decade. The proportion of the population aged over 65 is expected to rise from 18 per cent in 2024 to 27 per cent by 2075. The state pension and higher health and social care costs could mean ageing adds almost 10 per cent of GDP to fiscal pressures by 2075. Marginal taxes on a pensioner can reach as high as 60 per cent, but on a younger graduate they rise to 71 per cent. It also proposes a valuation tax on property across the board, set at a recommended rate of 0.65 per cent of the valuation. Outrage over new powers for an official valuation squad to inspect homes was reported this week, as a wealth tax on £2m homes comes into effect next year. If the token tax idea fails, Prof Ansell says redistribution via an “AI unearned rents tax” could be needed to sustain consumption across the economy.

events.summary: A Syrian entrepreneur who built his career in Dubai's e-commerce boom is betting that the same playbook of bundled services, one-tap payments and cashless transactions can help jump-start a market that international card networks abandoned for 14 years . “There are many successful examples in the UAE that help both locals and visitors,” said Rami Kaiem, co-founder of My Syria, a “super app” that lets visitors and residents book hotels, cars and tourist experiences and pay with Visa, Mastercard or Amex. “We are trying to repeat the success story we learnt from over the past 20 years in the UAE and apply it here in our country, Syria.” Mr Kaiem built the platform alongside co-founders Feras Kaiem, Waseem Qudmani and Kinan Madi through 121 Living, a UAE-based venture, after two decades working in the emirate's technology and logistics sector. The idea for My Syria was inspired by #MyDubai , a Dubai government-backed campaign promoting the city as a global destination, Mr Kaiem told The National in an interview. “As the owners of My Syria, we all hope to contribute to developing our country for the better and to apply here what we have learned from our experience in the UAE.” My Syria, which launched in Damascus earlier this month, is the first platform in Syria to process cross-border digital payments, a workaround in a country where Visa and Mastercard have only just begun re-establishing formal networks after being frozen out since 2011. The app signed up 12,000 active users in its first 15 days, Mr Kaiem said. “Anyone can now pay via Visa or Mastercard through our application. This is possible because our UAE-based company is able to receive the payments,” he said. “Dubai is very advanced when it comes to technology, e-commerce, infrastructure and logistics. We learnt a lot from the government, from the people and from the infrastructure there. That gave us a lot of experience in how to build a successful e-commerce business.” The Dubai experience is now being applied to a Syrian market where digital banking infrastructure is still nascent. The founders have promised Syria's Minister of Communications they will resolve the remaining gaps in international online payments within six months, Mr Kaiem said. Growing UAE ties Syria's economy is emerging from more than a decade of sanctions that cut it off from the global financial system, and Gulf capital is moving in fast to fill the vacuum. On Monday, the US removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, paving the way for international banking institutions and capital to re-enter the country. The UAE and Syria held their first bilateral business forum since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in May, when UAE Minister of Foreign Trade Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi led a delegation of officials and businessmen to Damascus. Gulf investors poured $28 billion into the Syrian economy in 2025. UAE logistics operator DP World has committed $800 million to a 30-year concession to run the port of Tartous on Syria's western Mediterranean coast. The World Bank puts Syria's reconstruction bill at $216 billion, which is roughly 10 times the country's 2024 gross domestic product. International payment companies are slowly making their way back. Mastercard signed a memorandum of understanding with the Central Bank of Syria in September 2025, the first agreement of its scale with the Syrian regulator since sanctions took hold. In January, the regulator licensed Qatar National Bank to resume card operations in the country. However, Syrian banks still carry more than $1.6 billion in exposure to Lebanon's financial crisis and have not been required to modernise compliance systems in more than a decade. My Syria is positioning itself to bridge that gap in the meantime, drawing directly on the model Mr Kaiem watched take shape in Dubai. The app currently offers eight services, including car rental, hotel bookings and holiday-home rentals, concentrated in Damascus, with plans to expand to roughly 40 services and eventually cover the whole country. Syria's Ministry of Tourism says visitor arrivals more than doubled in the first half of 2026, to 3.52 million from 1.67 million a year earlier, as the country reopens to travellers after Mr Assad's fall. “The journey with My Syria has just started,” Mr Kaiem said. “We have a lot of work to do.” For now, much of Syria's economy, and its tourism sector in particular, still runs offline and on cash, a legacy of sanctions. My Syria's founders are wagering that closing that gap, transaction by transaction, can make the app a digital front door for a country trying to convince Gulf money and foreign visitors that it is open for business.

events.title: Police investigate theft of 400,000 oysters in NSW
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Police investigate theft of 400,000 oysters from NSW farmer's Old Bar lease Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Ryan Freeman has been growing oysters for the last six years. ( Supplied: Ryan Freeman ) Police are investigating the theft of 400,000 oysters from leases on the NSW Mid North Coast. An oyster grower says he is back to square one, estimating as much as $400,000 worth of stock was stolen. NSW Police say they are investigating the alleged theft of $350,000 worth of oysters. Police are investigating after hundreds of thousands of oysters were stolen from leases on the New South Wales Mid North Coast. Ryan Freeman runs Latitude 31 Oysters, which operates leases on Scotts Creek at Oxley Island. Police said 320 aquaculture oyster bags containing 400,000 juvenile oysters were stolen from the property. Mr Freeman said he noticed the oysters were missing in the Manning River near Old Bar on Tuesday morning, when he went down to check on them to get them ready for Christmas. "We noticed our floating gear and tumblers were missing," he said. Police said the estimated value of the oysters was approximately $350,000. Mr Freeman said, in total, as much as $400,000 worth of stock and equipment was stolen. Ryan Freeman owns oyster leases in the Manning River, Karuah River and Port Stephens region. ( Supplied: Ryan Freeman ) Mr Freeman said 80 per cent of the stock stolen was going to be sold come Christmas time. "We probably get through 35-40,000 dozen at Christmas time," Mr Freeman said. "That’s why the thieves would have targeted them because they're not going to be far off, they're going to be able to sell them this Christmas." Mr Freeman said there was not enough time to look for more stock. The oyster leases are located on the New South Wales Mid North Coast at Manning Point. ( Supplied: Ryan Freeman ) Mr Freeman said he did not know how many oysters he had left, but so far he had lost a third of his livestock. "I understand everyone is doing it tough, but I don't believe stealing and taking from someone else is going to help someone else; all you've done is take someone else out for a small reward and high risk," he said. Police are urging anyone with information, including CCTV footage, to come forward. events.title: Commercial fishers frustrated with delays to compensation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA demersal fishers 'fighting tooth and nail' for compensation, nine months from ban Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Phil de Grauw has spent 40 years fishing in Kalbarri, and is one of a group of fishers who have hired a Melbourne law firm to negotiate with the government for compensation. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis ) Demersal fishers in WA are still waiting for compensation, nine months after the government shut down their industry along a 900-kilometre stretch of coast. Last week, the fisheries minister took over negotiations herself, ending an arrangement with a barrister who had been negotiating on the government's behalf. About half of the impacted fishing fleet have hired a Melbourne-based law firm to negotiate their share of a $20 million compensation package. Frustration is growing among Western Australia's demersal fishers, with many yet to see any compensation nine months after the state government shut down their industry. When it closed the West Coast demersal fishery, the government earmarked $20 million to compensate or "buy out" the commercial operators. According to fishers negotiating with the government, most affected by the closure are still awaiting compensation. However, negotiations have now taken a new turn, with Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis ending an arrangement with a Perth barrister tasked with negotiating compensation for the industry. The demersal fishery was closed due to sustainability concerns based on data for indicator species, including pink snapper. ( ABC News: Eliza Borrello ) Fishers' concerns about how long the process might take were heightened last week when an email was sent from the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development advising the fishers that negotiations would be directly with the minister. WA Fishing Industry Council chief executive Manue Daniels said there was a "hope" that the minister moving the negotiations in-house would speed up settlements, but she was seeking more information. "I've stressed to the minister we can't afford any more delays," she said. "It's nine months and they haven't been able to generate any income. It's not right. "At the very least, the government could have easily let them fish until the process of compensation was dealt with, or have the compensation process ready and everything done prior. "It is absolutely unacceptable to have people not being able to pay their bills, not being able to afford living and basic needs, and take that long to sort out the process." Manue Daniels says a nine-month wait for compensation is unacceptable. ( ABC News: Tara de Landgrafft ) Phil de Grauw has fished at Kalbarri for 40 years, working in both the West Coast and the Gascoyne demersal fisheries. He said about half of the displaced West Coast fishers had hired a Melbourne-based law firm to negotiate compensation with the government on their behalf. "We weren't confident with the approach, the consultation process or anything, and we received absolutely no information on how that compensation package might work," he said. Mr de Grauw said it was still unclear what sort of compensation he was entitled to, and he felt any money for many fishers was "months away". "It's a pretty long wait if you haven't been able to fish at all," he said. "A lot of guys have moved on, but there are a few that are relying on that money. "Some licence holders have already been paid out solely based on their licence value, but that is a minority." He said 30 wet-line boats and six shark boats had been forced off the water. Pink snapper were included in the ban due to sustainability issues. ( ABC News: Lauren Smith ) Mr de Grauw conceded the compensation process would be complicated for investors who leased fishing units to operators, as well as fishers who owned related businesses such as fish shops. "We can't pigeon-hole every fisher, we are all totally different … there's a real mix of the types of fishing, the size of the boats, the scale, and different bits and pieces that put together what is the wet-line fleet," he said. No chance of compensation for lessees While some are able to continue to negotiate for compensation, former Dongara fisher James Oliver will receive none of the money set aside for the industry. After working as a deckhand for years, he bought his own boat, leased fishing units and started his own wet-line business, supplying fresh fish to markets in Geraldton. But he said because he leased his fishing units, rather than owning them, he is not entitled to any compensation.

Mysterious disappearances have been taking place lately in Rutland, an East Midlands pocket between Leicestershire, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire that is often considered to be England’s smallest county . Usually, there are road signs when driving into a new county welcoming you over the border. But in recent months, these have been going missing. After 10 signs vanished, the council decided to remove the remaining 17. Now there are no official “Rutland” signs at all. The area’s MP, the Conservative Alicia Kearns, is “not sure” what the motivation behind the thefts is. But they are certainly a fitting metaphor for Rutland’s disappearing status: its council is due to merge with Leicestershire county council in spring 2028. Continue reading...

events.title: Why Tesla has been caught up in a massive car recall in China
events.summary: Hidden door handles were popularised by Tesla Hidden car door handles - the sleek designs often found on electric vehicles (EVs) - have come under the spotlight over the past week. That's after China announced its biggest ever recall of cars, with more than four million vehicles - mostly Teslas - affected . The recall comes ahead of new regulations in China , requiring cars to have a mechanical release both on the inside and outside of their doors. Popularised by Elon Musk's electric vehicle giant, this type of handle has become commonplace around the world. But several incidents have raised concerns that this design may make doors difficult to open in an emergency. Hidden door handles are widely used in modern cars in China, with around 60% of the top 100 best-selling new energy vehicles, including EVs and hybrids, having them. The minimalist design gives vehicles a "sleek look and reduces wind drag" but can be confusing to use, car industry analyst Stephen Dyer from consultancy AlixPartners told the BBC. "Even I often find it difficult to locate the switch to open the door from the inside of an unfamiliar vehicle," said Dyer, who is based in Shanghai. But beyond their usability, the handles have been blamed for endangering the lives of drivers and passengers. Electronically powered door handles became an industry trend, but raised "real safety concerns" when doors failed to open promptly, delaying rescue efforts after accidents, said Nanyang Technological University associate professor Lyu Chen. "A door handle may seem simple, but it becomes safety-critical in the seconds after a crash," Chen said. Chinese carmaker Xiaomi faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2025 involving its SU7 model, when suspected electrical failures allegedly trapped occupants. One of the incidents took place on a highway in Tongling city, eastern China, killing three people, according to regional news coverage cited by state-controlled media Global Times. Relatives of the victims said the passengers were stuck in the car as the vehicle's doors could not be unlocked after the collision, the outlet said. The SU7 was Xiaomi's first electric vehicle At the time, Xiaomi's representatives said the SU7 had mechanical emergency release handles that function even without power, which are located at the bottom of each door. The company added at the time that it was investigating the matter and cooperating with the police. The latest models of the SU7 come with new door handles that can be opened without power. Xiaomi has not responded to BBC requests for comment. Tesla has also faced lawsuits in the US over its door handle designs. The company has been sued by the only survivor of a crash in 2024 involving a Cybertruck - Tesla's electric pickup - that killed three college students in California. Survivor Jordan Miller alleged that the Cybertruck's design trapped passengers in the burning vehicle and blocked their rescue. The car did not have door handles and the electronic buttons meant to open the doors failed to work, according to his lawyers from The Veen Firm. "When you design a vehicle with no mechanical way to open the doors from the outside, you are betting the electronics will work in every scenario, including a high-speed crash followed by a fire," said one of the lawyers in a statement. In court filings, Tesla denied any wrongdoing and said the Cybertruck is compliant with US federal safety standards, the Guardian reported. There have been other cases in the US of passengers, including children, allegedly being trapped in Tesla cars after the doors suddenly stopped working. The BBC has contacted Tesla for comment. What is being done about hidden handles? In February, China said it would ban hidden door handles, making it the first country to do so. The new rules, which take effect on 1 January 2027, mean new car designs without physical release mechanisms on the inside and outside of their doors cannot be sold. The cars' interior must also carry signs to show how to open the door. The measures in China come ahead of the US and European Union, which typically lead regulations around road safety and emissions, Dyer noted. One reason is likely to be the sheer number of EVs in China, he added. On 21 August, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced that Tesla and some major Chinese car makers - including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely - would recall more than four million vehicles. China will ban hidden door handles on cars sold in the country from next year The manufacturers were ordered to add warning labels inside vehicle doors to show passengers how to open them. Some cars will also get a software update that will lower their windows in the event of a crash. Tesla, which started selling the Model S sedan with hidden door handles in China in 2014, is recalling nearly three million cars, according to the SAMR.

events.title: Graham wins South Carolina Senate primary, vindicating Trump
events.summary: The News South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s primary for a full term, riding President Donald Trump’s endorsement to a narrow victory after a quick special election. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” Graham said of Trump at her victory party in Columbia. She immediately pivoted to the general election against Democrat Annie Andrews, warning that she advocates “turning confused little boys into little girls and vice versa.” Graham, who’d never sought office before being appointed to replace her brother Lindsey in the Senate, was backed by most of the state’s GOP leadership, and her allies — including MAGA Inc., the president’s super PAC — outspent her primary competitor, Rep. Ralph Norman. “We had $8 million spent against us,” Norman told his supporters, bemoaning the president’s decision to endorse Graham. “His policies are good. I never understood why he got in this race. It is what it is.” Graham built an insurmountable lead in the 7th Congressional District in and around Myrtle Beach, where Rep. Russell Fry endorsed her after losing his own Senate bid, and where the president flew in for a weekend rally. Norman carried his district and the upstate, where the Grahams were raised and where conservative voters had been most critical of the late senator. In the rest of the state, Graham prevailed — including in the Charleston area, where former governor and congressman Mark Sanford endorsed Norman after his own Senate campaign faltered. She linked herself directly to the president, telling voters that, unlike her brother, she’d get rid of the filibuster to pass Trump’s voter ID law, and said she’d never support amnesty for undocumented immigrants. The president was on the verge of getting another endorsee over the line in Oklahoma, where former state Sen. Mike Mazzei beat Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the runoff for the GOP nomination for governor. Mazzei did best with votes cast on Election Day, after Drummond had criticized the president’s plan to import beef to ameliorate the effects of his tariffs. “When he gets it wrong, I will speak up,” Drummond said of Trump. David’s view Graham’s campaign, powered by her brother’s old political operation, impressed Republicans. Graham’s candidacy sometimes didn’t. After last week’s only runoff debate, where the senator punted a question on Taiwan and explained that “foreign policy” wasn’t her expertise, Republicans upped their expectations for Norman, a House Freedom Caucus member who ran to Graham’s right. But she won, and the president got to claim another victory, which she was happy to attribute to him. His intervention in Oklahoma was just as impressive: Mazzei, whose top issue is ending the state income tax, didn’t have a political legacy to run on like Graham’s. Notable Ben Jacobs covered the final days of the South Carolina runoff for Slate, including the in-person Myrtle Beach rally that the president attended: “It’s never an ideal sign when a candidate’s support at an election-eve rally is less than unanimous.”

events.title: Why rising heat is Asia’s next major health challenge
events.summary: Higher temperatures are putting new pressure on health systems across the region, prompting a broader push for awareness, prevention and earlier action Across the globe – and Asia in particular – the link between a changing climate and human health is becoming harder to ignore. Home to an estimated 60 per cent of the world’s population, Asia is warming faster than the global average and ranks among the planet’s most climate-disaster-prone regions. Yet public awareness has not kept pace with the scale of the threat. In Hong Kong, many residents remain unaware of the health risks posed by rising temperatures; they are also unaware of how simple behavioural changes could help reduce their exposure. Densely populated cities face particular risks. Concrete-heavy urban environments can trap heat, while air pollution, changing disease patterns and extreme weather events add to the burden. In 2024, Hong Kong recorded its hottest year on record, with 52 “very hot days” and 50 “hot nights”. This month, the city witnessed its hottest day on record. The “Climate and Health in Asia” report, produced by Forum for the Future and sponsored by AIA, describes extreme heat as a growing threat to population health. The risks are particularly acute in cities, where polluted air and the urban heat-island effect can compound exposure and keep temperatures elevated after sunset, prolonging exposure and endangering those most at risk. Asia’s rapidly ageing population must also be considered. By 2050, one in four people in the region are expected to be over 60, according to the report, increasing healthcare demand just as climate-related risks accelerate. “Human health is strongly determined by environmental health,” says Emily Chan, assistant dean and professor of Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Faculty of Medicine. “With climate change, there is a direct, visible and palpable impact on the population in Hong Kong. Research here shows that temperature extremes, sudden changes and especially summer heat have specific effects on mortality and morbidity across a range of diseases, as well as on the ability of the health system to cope.” Hot nights intensify the problem. “Research in Hong Kong found that a 24-hour cycle gives the community a chance to recover if nights are cooler than the daytime,” Chan says. “When the evening cooling period is shortened or disappears during periods of extreme heat, the risk multiplies for the general population, especially for vulnerable groups.” For Amita Chaudhury, AIA’s group head of sustainability and chair of the United Nations Principles for Sustainable Insurance Board, one of the biggest challenges is that climate-related health risks continue to be seen in isolation. “Climate change is still largely viewed as an environmental issue, yet factors such as extreme heat, poor air quality and severe weather are increasingly affecting the health and well-being of communities,” she says. “Many people see it as an inconvenience rather than a health risk, yet prolonged exposure can affect cardiovascular health, respiratory conditions, mental well-being and overall quality of life – particularly among older adults and those with pre-existing health conditions.” Globally, heat-related mortality among people over 65 has risen sharply compared with the 1990s, according to evidence cited in the report. For ageing societies such as Hong Kong’s, the trend highlights the need to treat extreme heat as something that is more than a seasonal inconvenience. “Research on temperature and health already shows that beyond certain thresholds, hospital admissions and deaths increase, depending on the disease,” Chan says. “If we consider the increasing number of hot days in the city over the past five years, there is good reason to believe that silent mortality and health service demand are increasing as well.” Heat is often described as a “silent disaster” – unlike a typhoon, heat does not always produce a clear moment of impact or trigger an equally visible community response. Yet the effects can accumulate across homes, workplaces, schools and hospitals. Chan says Hong Kong has the building blocks required for a stronger response, including reliable health data, skilled healthcare workers and the capacity to cope with emergencies. The challenge is ensuring these resources can be mobilised in real time when temperatures reach dangerous levels. The climate-health challenge also creates an opportunity to strengthen preparedness before illness occurs. Historically, healthcare protection has focused largely on treatment and recovery. Chaudhury says there is now a need to place greater emphasis on awareness, prevention and engagement to help people build resilience before health issues arise. AIA’s programmes reflect this broader shift towards prevention and long-term well-being.

events.title: Musk's rocket firm SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility
events.summary: Musk's SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility in Louisiana SpaceX already has facilities in Texas and Florida Multi-billionaire Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX has announced that it will build its largest launch site yet in the southern US state of Louisiana. Construction of the $100bn (£73bn) project - named Starbase, Louisiana - is due to start next year, with the 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site expanding on the company's operations beyond its current Texas headquarters and locations in Florida. It will be used to "support thousands of Starship flights a year with missions launching to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond," SpaceX said on Tuesday. In June, SpaceX shares started trading on New York's technology-focused Nasdaq in the world's biggest ever stock market debut . SpaceX said it aims to launch its first Starship flight from the new Louisiana base in 2029. The facility will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region, the company said , external . The Louisiana Economic Development agency said the average wage of workers at the base - the largest of its kind in the world - would be 192% more than the region's current average salary. It will also create more than 8,100 new jobs indirectly, the agency estimated. "The historic project will establish Louisiana as a global hub for next-generation aerospace, with the capacity and infrastructure needed to dramatically increase launch frequency and expand access to space," it added. The facility in Louisiana will share its name with another SpaceX site on the southern tip of Texas. In 2025, residents in an area of Cameron County, where the company has testing and development operations, approved incorporating the patch of land as a city called Starbase . Inside the rural Texas town where Elon Musk is basing his business empire Published 20 April 2025 The SpaceX IPO made history. One month on has it lost momentum? Published 13 July Musk has set out ambitious goals for SpaceX, including plans to reach Mars, develop artificial intelligence (AI) models and launch data centres into space. In August, SpaceX and Tesla - Musk's electric vehicle and robotics firm - announced plans to build a $16.8bn artificial intelligence (AI) chip making complex in Texas called the Terafab. The facility aims to meet the companies' growing demand for computing power to support its projects including developing AI and robotics technology over the coming years. The newly-listed SpaceX is under pressure to convince investors that it will be profitable even as it pursues its expansion plans. Its shares have tumbled by more than 30% from the highs reached shortly after it began trading but are still higher than their $135 offer price. events.title: Court ruling threatens Republicans' midterm TV ad advantage
events.summary: A federal appeals court ruling Tuesday could erase a new midterm advantage for Republicans. Why it matters: The 2-1 ruling would block Republicans from using cash-rich party committees to buy more political TV ads at discounted rates. Republicans plan to appeal the decision, setting up another high-stakes campaign finance fight as the fall ad wars heat up ahead of November. Driving the news: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled the FCC was wrong to extend discounted candidate broadcast rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees that include non-candidate groups for ads they coordinate with candidates. The rates paid by super PACs and other outside groups are often several times higher than candidate rates. The case was brought by four Democratic candidates running this cycle — Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), former Gov. Roy Cooper (N.C.) and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (Mich.) The U.S. Supreme Court in June struck down limits on how much committees can spend in coordination with campaigns. Between the lines: Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance extending candidate rates to certain coordinated ads, would allow party committee cash to stretch further. The ruling applied to both parties. But while Democratic candidates generally have stronger grassroots fundraising, Republican Party committees have amassed larger war chests, fueled by megadonors Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance, allowed party committee cash to stretch further by accessing lower rates reserved for candidates. What they're saying: "Put plainly, today's ruling makes clear that lowest unit rate is an exclusive right given to candidates and incumbent campaigns and that is the law of the land," DSCC executive director Devan Barber and DCCC executive director Julie Merz said in a joint statement. "Democratic candidates' strong grassroots fundraising amplifying the voice of everyday Americans remains a fundamental advantage in the midterms," they continued. "This was an incorrect ruling that ignores decades of precedent," NRSC communications director Joanna Rodriguez said in a statement. "We plan on appealing and this is the first word not the last," she continued.

events.title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP Senate runoff
events.summary: Sen. Darline Graham , President Trump's endorsed candidate, won the Republican nomination Tuesday to fill the Senate vacancy created by her brother Lindsey Graham 's death, per the AP. Why it matters: The victory underscores Trump's continued sway with Republican voters and positions Graham as the odds-on favorite to win a full term in November. Graham, 62, will be heavily favored against Democrat Annie Andrews in November . Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in South Carolina since 1998. Driving the news : Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman finished first and second , respectively, in the Aug. 11 primary and advanced to Tuesday's runoff after neither won the majority needed to secure the nomination outright. Graham entered the race July 20, days after Gov. Henry McMaster (R) appointed her to serve temporarily in the seat held by her late brother — her first time holding elected office. Her abbreviated primary campaign benefited from Trump's endorsement, the advantages of incumbency and one of the most recognizable names in South Carolina politics. In addition to campaigning with Graham in South Carolina on Friday, MAGA Inc. made a last-minute push for her, spending more than $827,000 on phone calls and text messages ahead of Tuesday's vote, according to FEC reports. Zoom in: Graham's statement during a runoff debate that she was "not that informed on national security," in response to a question about U.S. policy toward Taiwan, fueled questions about her readiness for the job. It also highlighted the contrast with her late brother, who for decades was a Senate leader on foreign policy and national security matters. Norman posted on X : "South Carolina deserves a Senator who UNDERSTANDS Foreign Policy. I'm a PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH supporter! No more forever wars!" The other side : Norman, 73, argued that Republican voters should judge candidates by their records, presenting himself as a proven conservative rather than a first-time candidate elevated by a famous name. A hard-line conservative, Norman is vice chair of the House Freedom Caucus. In June, Norman placed third in South Carolina's Republican gubernatorial primary, behind Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette and Alan Wilson, the state's attorney general. Between the lines : Both Graham and Norman flooded the airwaves, spending a combined total of more than $5 million on ads during the primary runoff, according to AdImpact. "Stand with President Trump. Vote Darline Graham for Senate," one pro-Graham ad stated, while another accused Norman of being a "career politician." "This election is not for sale," Norman said in one ad. "South Carolina needs a proven conservative with a record of fighting for you. You shouldn't have to guess where your next senator stands. With me, you already know."

events.title: The widening divide between cyber threats and cyber defenses
events.summary: The patch window is collapsing: Why security needs a new control plane For decades, cybersecurity defenders have relied on a relatively straightforward model: a vulnerability is disclosed, security teams assess exposure, test available fixes, deploy patches into production, and ultimately close the risk before attackers can exploit it at scale. That model increasingly reflects a world that no longer exists. Today’s enterprises operate thousands of interconnected workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. Mission-critical applications power revenue-generating services, customer experiences, and core business operations that cannot simply be taken offline whenever a security update becomes available. At the same time, vulnerabilities are becoming more visible, more widely distributed, and more rapidly weaponized than ever before. The result is a growing gap between how quickly organizations can safely remediate vulnerabilities and how quickly adversaries can exploit them. It is time to rethink how the industry approaches security during the critical period between disclosure and remediation. Traditional vulnerability management was built on the assumption that defenders could move faster than attackers. In many cases, they could. When a vulnerability was disclosed, organizations had time to understand the issue, assess affected systems, test patches, coordinate change windows, and deploy fixes before widespread exploitation occurred. Today that timeline is rapidly shrinking. Modern attack campaigns operate at internet scale. Security research, public disclosures, proof-of-concept exploits, and threat intelligence circulate globally within hours. A vulnerability announced in the morning can become the focus of active scanning and exploitation efforts by the afternoon. Meanwhile, the operational realities of enterprise environments have not changed. Organizations still must: Understand the vulnerability and its business impact. Identify affected systems across large estates. Evaluate dependencies and compatibility concerns. Validate fixes in test environments. Monitor for regressions and operational risk. These are not signs of inefficiency. They are necessary safeguards for business-critical environments. The challenge is that while defensive processes continue to require days or weeks, offensive timelines are increasingly measured in hours. That creates one of the most dangerous periods in modern cybersecurity: the window between awareness and remediation. AI is expanding the defender’s challenge AI is helping organizations modernize operations, accelerate development, and improve security outcomes. But the same technological advances are also changing the economics of offensive operations. Historically, transforming a newly disclosed vulnerability into an effective attack often required extensive manual research and deep technical expertise. Security researchers and attackers alike needed to analyze documentation, understand exploit conditions, study affected software, and develop attack techniques. Many of those steps can now be accelerated. AI-assisted workflows can help analyze vulnerability disclosures, identify likely attack paths, evaluate technical dependencies, and summarize complex technical information far more quickly than traditional manual processes. As these capabilities become more accessible, the timeline between disclosure and exploitation continues to compress. The result is a structural imbalance. Defenders remain responsible for protecting entire environments that may include thousands of servers, applications, databases, containers, and network assets. Attackers only need to identify a single viable path to exploitation. This asymmetry is driving organizations to ask an increasingly important question: What happens before the patch is deployed? Why existing security approaches fall short The security industry has invested heavily in improving visibility. Organizations today have access to more vulnerability data, threat intelligence, analytics, and detection capabilities than ever before. Security platforms can rapidly identify affected systems, prioritize remediation, and alert defenders to emerging threats. These capabilities are essential. But awareness alone does not reduce exposure. Many organizations find themselves in a position where they know exactly which systems are vulnerable but cannot immediately patch them. For example, a business-critical application may require extensive validation before updates can be deployed. A manufacturing system may depend on software that cannot be taken offline during production hours. A regulated environment may require additional testing and approval processes before changes can be implemented. In these situations, the challenge is not identifying risk. The challenge is reducing risk while remediation is still underway. Visibility, detection, and prioritization help organizations understand the problem. They do not necessarily provide a mechanism for containing that risk immediately. As attack timelines continue to compress, the industry needs a complementary approach focused on exposure reduction rather than simply exposure awareness. Why the network is emerging as the fastest control plane When a workload cannot immediately defend itself, another layer must help provide protection. Increasingly, organizations are looking to the network. Unlike endpoint-based controls, network-level protections operate around workloads rather than inside them. This distinction becomes particularly important during periods of elevated risk. The network already understands communication patterns, connectivity requirements, trust relationships, and traffic flows. It sits at a strategic position where organizations can influence how systems interact with one another without necessarily modifying the applications themselves. This creates opportunities to reduce exploitability while remediation efforts are underway. Network-enforced protections can help: Restrict access to vulnerable systems. Limit exposure to potential attack paths. Reduce opportunities for lateral movement. Adjust controls dynamically as new information becomes available. Perhaps most importantly, network controls can often be implemented significantly faster than enterprise software patches can be validated and deployed. The objective is not to avoid patching. The objective is to create a meaningful layer of defense during the period when patching has not yet been completed. As AI compresses the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation, organizations need a defensive layer that can act immediately, without waiting for every workload to be patched, every application to be modified, or every endpoint agent to understand a new threat.

events.title: Super-rich losing millions as some Hong Kong trophy homes sell at painful discounts
events.summary: Under-pressure owners are cutting prices to exit Hong Kong’s luxury property market, with some homes losing more than HK$100 million in value Hong Kong has seen a string of cut-price deals for super-luxury homes in recent months, with financially pressured owners accepting eye-watering losses to exit the market even as demand for trophy homes remains strong. Among the latest examples is the sale of a Bel-Air luxury house for HK$138 million (US$17.6 million), about HK$37 million below the price the former owner paid for the property in 2018. The 3,792 sq ft house in Pok Fu Lam was bought for HK$175 million in 2018 by Shie Thomas, according to Land Registry records. Shie reportedly has ties to the Hong Kong export firm Tak Fi International, and is also listed as a racehorse owner by the Hong Kong Jockey Club. An agreement to sell the property for HK$138 million was signed in June between the property’s latest owner, Shie Serena She-wing, and a buyer named as Chen Dongqiong, with the assignment registered on August 18. The transaction represents a more than 20 per cent loss on the 2018 purchase price. Land Registry records also show the property was mortgaged to Dah Sing Bank in 2022, with a rental assignment subsequently registered in favour of the bank. The Bel-Air sale is not an isolated case. Several high-end houses and flats have recently changed hands well below their previous purchase prices, showing that a revival in luxury home sales in Hong Kong has not necessarily helped every owner recover their equity. At The Morgan on Conduit Road, a nearly 4,000 sq ft home with a private terrace sold for HK$190 million, a painful 45 per cent below the HK$344 million paid by the previous owner in 2018, according to Land Registry records. events.title: Rubio tells allies U.S. shifting from strikes to sanctions on Iran
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has told several of his foreign counterparts in recent days that "for the time being" the U.S. is not expected to initiate new strikes against Iran , according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Instead, he's said the focus is on other means of pressure, including the sanctions initiative announced this week. Why it matters: Rubio's message to foreign ministers from several allied countries comes as the U.S. believes it's suffocating Iran with the naval blockade — while moving ever-increasing amounts of oil out of the Strait of Hormu z. It's also another sign that President Trump is exasperated with the war and wants it to be over, at least for now. The U.S. official said that while Rubio made clear that the U.S. isn't planning a return to major combat operations, he didn't rule out strikes if Iran attacks first. Another U.S. official said the clearing of mines from the Strait of Hormuz by the U.S. Navy is a watershed moment in the war, largely neutralizing one of Iran's main sources of leverage. Behind the scenes: The sources said Rubio outlined the Trump administration's current Iran policy in phone calls with several of his counterparts: Avoiding military action against Iran for the time being. Increasing economic pressure on Iran through the U.S. naval blockade and the new Treasury Department sanctions push. Transporting as much oil as possible through the strait and into global energy markets. A second U.S. official said this is expected to be the policy at least until after the midterm elections, when a new military campaign could again be on the table. State of play: U.S. officials say the clearing of mines from most of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with the fact that more and more tankers have been moving through the southern lane of the strait in recent weeks, significantly reduces Iran's leverage over global energy markets. "The Iranians have lost control over the strait. Now the U.S. controls it," one U.S. official said. The U.S. naval blockade is depriving Iran of critical revenue. Over the last two weeks, almost no tankers have been spotted at Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export hub, U.S. officials say. "The Iranian economy is in free fall and the regime's military has been decimated," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told Axios, "and we are cutting off every financial lifeline the regime has remaining." He added, "The President has been clear that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, and that he will use the tools necessary to ensure that objective is accomplished." The big picture: Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, was in Tehran on Sunday for talks with the Iranian leadership. Pakistan has been a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran since the war began. According to Al Arabiya, the Saudi-affiliated TV station, Munir spoke to Trump before the trip and suggested a new proposal for the Iranians. The White House didn't deny that Trump spoke to Munir but said there are no current or scheduled negotiations with Iran. U.S. officials say that the new developments in the strait and the growing volume of oil coming out of the Gulf have deprived Iran of a major card in any future negotiations and made any potential deal between Oman and Iran regarding the strait irrelevant. "Right now we are not negotiating with Iran. We are squeezing them. The pressure could drive the Iranians back to the table," a U.S. official said. What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have been leading the negotiations with Iran, are expected to visit U.S. Central Command on Wednesday for briefings on the situation on the ground, according to a source with knowledge.

events.title: Canada strikes back with tit-for-tat tariffs
events.summary: Canadian officials announced they plan to impose tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods in retaliation for new US levies. The tariffs will mostly mirror President Donald Trump’s, with the heftiest affecting steel and aluminum. “When the United States asked too much and offered too little, we chose to stand up for Canadians,” said François-Philippe Champagne, Canada’s finance minister. The move heightens the stakes for congressional Republicans in states that border Canada, many of whom are already taking heat for rising prices ahead of midterms. “If you are a Midwestern-northern state with a big auto industry, or you rely on Canadian tourism … I can’t imagine this is helpful,” Ernst & Young’s Blake Harden, former GOP trade counsel for the House Ways and Means Committee, told Semafor. “I don’t think this is the thing they really want to be talking about.” It could be worse: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said earlier this week that “everything on the table,” including surcharges on electricity Canada exports to the US. That would hit states like Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is in a close reelection race, especially hard. Still, voters nationally are already grappling with higher energy and technology costs, which may make them hypersensitive to any additional price increases. “Everything this year just feels more expensive,” Center on Budget and Policy Priorities Chief Economist Gbenga Ajilore told Semafor. “Now, that’s just going to make it even more expensive.” Canada announced a $7.5 billion aid package for companies affected by the trade war, suggesting Ottawa is preparing for a prolonged fight. But Canadian tariffs won’t take effect till Sept. 8, which gives officials some time to restart negotiations. “It does create some space,” Harden said. “I think the hope, on all sides, is that the two governments get back to the table.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Addressing a sticking point in sustainable adhesives
events.summary: Stephanie M. McPherson, SM ’11 archive page Petroleum-based adhesives are everywhere: bonding the wood and drywall in a construction project, holding together the joints of furniture, and even sticking labels to otherwise recyclable containers. “The labels on a container are held up with petroleum-based glue. And because of that, even though you’re putting the container in the recycle bin, it will not get recycled,” says Patty Ferreira, MBA ’97, CEO and cofounder of Silvis Materials, which is combating this problem with its fully biodegradable cellulose adhesives. When Ferreira began thinking about bio-based adhesives, in 2014, she started by modifying cellulose’s existing role as a stabilizer in adhesive emulsions and replicating the known adhesive properties of more expensive nanocellulose. Today, the formula can make adhesives from virtually every type of plant cellulose, and the MIT Startup Exchange (STEX) is helping Silvis work with packaging and construction companies to test the results. She expects the adhesive to cut production emissions by up to 80% and use half the energy of fossil-based glues. This story was part of our September/October 2026 issue. events.title: YouTuber finds niche as college admissions mentor
events.summary: As a first-generation student from a small town, Gohar Khan ’21 had to navigate the college admissions process largely on his own. He founded his YouTube channel, Gohar’s Guide, to make things easier for other young people. Today, more than 10 million people follow Khan on social media for college application advice, study tips, and life hacks. He is also the CEO and cofounder of Next Admit, a consulting business that provides help with college essays, applications, and test preparation. “I’m on a mission to help students worldwide succeed inside and outside of school,” he says. events.title: Launching youth entrepreneurship
events.summary: Even as a teenager, Laurie Stach ’06 says, she had a “crazy ambition to take on the world and solve problems.” At MIT, she realized she wasn’t the only one. “Adults always see these youth who are good at math and science and say, ‘You’re going to do great things—someday,’” says Stach. “Meanwhile, traditional education isn’t preparing them.” That’s why in 2012 Stach founded LaunchX, a for-profit entrepreneurship program that helps high school students build practical skills through an intensive summer program in which they start real companies. Stach says that students form teams, identify a problem, and build an actual product or service that they then take to market—often generating preorders or even revenue before the four-week program ends. Raised in Texas and the Carolinas, Stach majored in mechanical engineering at MIT and earned her MBA from Harvard Business School in 2011. She ran her first summer program on MIT’s campus with 30 students in 2013 and says “it kind of snowballed.” LaunchX now serves about 500 students per year across both in-person and online programs . events.title: A new stamp on cyberfraud prevention
events.summary: For Rupert Young ’95, SM ’95, his career in data science and cybersecurity began when his grandfather gifted him thousands of stamps: He built intricate databases to catalogue them, displaying the “precise eye” for detail and nuance that his MIT application essay said would make him a good engineer. Young is now chief product officer of ­MaxMind, whose work with IP-address location data and fraud prevention has made it a go-to resource. Streaming companies, security vendors, merchants, and ad-network providers use its signature tool, GeoIP, to determine how and where users are accessing services. This information makes it possible to ensure retail sites are using the correct currency, flag suspicious bank logins, and more. Young’s passion for engineering was shaped by internships, and he has paid it forward by volunteering at his children’s California high school and trying to keep up with what “the next generation of engineers are tinkering with.” The next generation of product innovation at MaxMind excites him too. “Working with my team to try to find patterns in data and solve challenging problems—to me, there’s no greater joy,” he says. events.title: AgeLab research inspires an A I startup
events.summary: When Don Yansen ’63 arrived at the MIT AgeLab for a study on technology in care­giving for older adults, he didn’t plan to launch another company. But when he heard participants talk about how hard modern devices can be to use, he decided to develop an alternative. Yansen, a serial entrepreneur who retired to care for his wife, earned an MIT degree in electrical engineering and a master’s in physics from Northeastern. “What I took from MIT was a good education and the feeling I could solve difficult problems,” he says. One such problem: Many older adults “can’t even use a modern cell phone,” he says, “and very few people can use something like an Apple Watch.” So Kiwi Health, which he founded in October 2024, sells a wristband controlled primarily by voice. Wearers can set reminders, make calls, send texts, and share health data, all without navigating screens. AI helps interpret these commands, accounting for the way voices may change with age. The device also measures health metrics and automatically alerts caregivers to falls. Yansen’s hope, he says, is that it can “help seniors live the best life that they can.” This story was part of our September/October 2026 issue. events.title: Trump administration violated court order on mail-voting rules, judge says
events.summary: A Massachusetts judge ruled Tuesday that the Trump administration violated a nationwide injunction by finalizing a rule that would significantly overhaul mail voting if allowed to take effect. Why it matters: The order allows the Trump administration to publish the rule Wednesday, but the U.S. Postal Service remains barred from making the dramatic changes to mail-in ballots. Driving the news: "Defendants cannot contend that they misunderstood the scope of the court's order, " U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a five-page filing Tuesday afternoon. "Accordingly, despite the Defendants' protestations that '[t]he United States takes its obligation to comply with court orders very seriously,' the court finds that Defendants violated the preliminary injunction in this case." Catch up quick: Tuesday's ruling came in response to a motion from the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts asking Talwani to enforce her nationwide injunction blocking the new mail-ballot rules. The injunction bars the administration from directing USPS to reject ballot mail that doesn't comply with the administration's new design requirements until after the 2026 midterms. It also bars the administration from "initiating or completing rulemaking" to implement the new criteria. Yes, but: Talwani declined to implement any of the remedies the LWV requested. Zoom in: The Trump administration argued in an Aug. 25 filing that publishing the new rule did not violate the nationwide injunction because the rule's language specifically says the USPS won't implement the rule while the injunction is in place. Therefore, merely publishing the rule doesn't violate Talwani's order. The administration also insists that the final rule needed an effective date before the midterms so states would have enough time to comply if the injunction were lifted. Zoom out: The administration also argued that the Supreme Court's ruling Monday in a separate challenge to Trump's mail-voting executive order undercuts Talwani's preliminary injunction. SCOTUS paused a separate injunction Monday, finding the 23 states and D.C. could not challenge the impending policy before the rulemaking process was completed. The justices explicitly said the states could challenge USPS' final rule if it harms them, but found the states lacked standing because any alleged harm hadn't yet happened. The government argues that reasoning means Talwani should not have issued the preliminary injunction and should now vacate it. Talwani did not address the administration's reasoning regarding the Supreme Court's newest order, nor did she decide whether to lift the preliminary injunction. What we're watching: The coalition of states involved in the Supreme Court case is expected to sue the administration once the final rule is published. events.title: 'Stop with the manifestos', OpenAI's former communications director says
events.summary: Hannah Wong, a former communications lead at OpenAI , says technology executives need to stop writing long-winded essays and start telling the community how their products will help people. Ms Wong made the comments during an event organised by Clipbook, a media intelligence platform. The discussion focused on communications in the age of AI . "Companies need to do more showing and less telling," she told Clipbook founder and chief executive Adam Joseph, who moderated the discussion. "This is why these manifestos can fall flat. We don't want to hear anything any more." Ms Wong said that too many communications firms and professionals working in technology were releasing long essays on various topics. "Just yesterday I read one and then somebody sent me another. Can we stop with it?" she said. "I think these manifestos can fall flat when you say one thing and it's aspirational. For example, a lot of executives say AI will create opportunities for all of us, but on another hand you just laid off just a couple thousand people from the workforce." She said the mixed messages create a credibility gap and that far too many technology companies did not have people organising in the community and contacting influencers to help gain trust with a wider audience. "You're never going to win an argument by just talking at people," she explained. Her comments come weeks after Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg tried to turn around the increasingly negative public perception about AI by writing an essay. Many outlets referred to Mr Zuckerberg's essay of more than 6,000 words, titled "The Future is for Everyone", as a manifesto. Due to concerns about AI's potential to disrupt the labour market, harm the environment and be misused, AI companies such as OpenAI , Anthropic and Meta have faced ample scrutiny and been viewed with distrust. Ms Wong said that from her perspective, Airbnb and Nvidia seem to be better at connecting with audiences. "I think Brian Chesky is an amazing storyteller, and when you hear him speak it's very authentic," she said, referring to the Airbnb co-founder and chief executive. She echoed the sentiments of Mr Joseph, who spoke highly of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang 's ability to articulate how AI will improve society. "He's fantastic and it shows that we can do a better job in the industry of kind of finding those use-cases of AI and holding them up like a beacon," Ms Wong said. "It's that classic idea of showing and not telling." Ms Wong, who left OpenAI at the start of the year, said that during her time there, chief executive Sam Altman, was authentic, approachable and always willing to get the opinion of OpenAI's communications team. "I was really glad to have that sort of relationship with all the leaders of OpenAI," she said.

events.title: House Democrats' pro-Israel wing gains power on panel overseeing foreign policy
events.summary: A trio of vocally pro-Israel House Democrats were given powerful posts on the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday, with one taking the reins of the subcommittee that oversees U.S.-Middle East policy. Why it matters: It is a substantial win for the party's pro-Israel wing despite growing pro-Palestinian sentiment among the party's grassroots. And it could have global ramifications, with Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) indicating that, if he becomes chair of the Middle East and North Africa subcommittee next year, he will use the position to shore up U.S. support for Israel. "If Democrats take control of the House, I'll be in a position to help steer U.S. policy on Israel and the Middle East," he told Axios. Driving the news: In addition to Moskowitz leading Democrats on the MENA subcommittee, pro-Israel Reps. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) and Wesley Bell (D-Mo.) were appointed to the Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday. Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wisc.), a pro-Palestinian progressive and prolific critic of the pro-Israel group AIPAC, was also appointed to the panel. Moskowitz , Wasserman Schultz and Bell all dispatched left-wing primary challengers this election cycle who went after their support of Israel. What they're saying: Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, said the appointees' "experience, commitment, and expertise will strengthen our work and help guide the committee as it addresses urgent challenges in national security and diplomacy." "I look forward to working closely with all of our members during this turbulent time when Congressional oversight is most needed," added Meeks, who is also a vocal supporter of Israel.

events.title: Global economy so far resisting Iran war energy shock, IMF chief says
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund 's (IMF) managing director said on Tuesday that the global economy is faring better than expected as energy supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz drive uncertainty, although she warned of rising fiscal pressures. Energy supply disruptions from the Middle East put a new strain on a global economy facing stubborn inflation, rising debt levels and lingering trade tensions. Traffic disruption in the waterway, through which roughly 20 per cent of the world's energy supplies transited before the Iran war began in February, have gyrated oil prices, leading to mounting concerns over price pressures. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said a number of factors are helping the global economy to “resist” these disruptions, including a drawdown of oil and gas reserves , increases in non-Gulf supply, demand reductions and “some reversal back to coal”. Most recent projections from the fund expect the global economy to expand at a 3 per cent clip this year, slightly lower than its 3.1 per cent forecast in April. At the same time, it further downgraded its 2026 forecast for the Middle East to 0.7 per cent growth, 1.2 percentage points lower than in April. “Thus far, it has weathered the energy shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz better than we feared,” Ms Georgieva told reporters at the fund's headquarters before the G20 conference in North Carolina next week. Also partly accounting for this better-than-expected growth performance is the AI boom. The IMF chief said the benefits from this boom are now reaching beyond the US, while the net impact between the technological boom and the energy supply crisis is having an asymmetric impact across different countries. Global growth is expected to recover to 3.4 per cent next year, the IMF reported in July. “What started out as a US phenomenon with AI is now becoming a growth engine for the global economy,” she said. “We have a tug of war between the negative supply shock from the Middle East and the positive demand shock from AI.” Ms Georgieva said rising bond yields are evidence of rising fiscal pressures, placing new anxiety on markets and policymakers. The US Treasury Department last week announced it would at least double the size of its government debt repurchases after long-term yields reached their highest levels in 20 years. Separate US government data last week showed that US national debt surpassed $40 trillion – double what it was in 2017. “All countries need to tackle their fiscal problems and formulate and present credible plans to ensure their debt and deficits are on a sustainable path,” she said.

events.title: Kennedy Center's survival depends on Trump, DOJ says in new filing
events.summary: The Trump administration argued in a Monday court filing that the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts must undergo proposed renovations and a cash infusion to survive. Why it matters: It's the latest in the legal battle over the venue's future, which the administration has proposed to overhaul , including potentially adding President Trump's name to the building. Driving the news: "An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump," the DOJ argued in Monday's filing , "will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop." Without Trump's efforts, the filing reads, "the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down." The document also suggests that if the venue deteriorated that way, the Kennedy Center could be replaced with "a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River." Such a venue has "been proposed, by some, for many years," it continued. Catch up quick: The filing came in response to Rep. Joyce Beatty's (D-Ohio) request for a federal judge to block the Kennedy Center's board from trying once again to put Trump's name on the building. In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper ordered Trump's name removed from the building after its Trump-chaired board, stacked with MAGA allies, voted to rename it "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts." Yes, but: Earlier this month, the board pushed forward once again with plans to put the president's name on the center. Cooper said only Congress could change the center's name — but the DOJ argued in Monday's filing that the updated plan would not rename the center. Rather, the board's recent vote approved an inscription under the center's name that would read "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump," while the physical site would be renamed the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." State of play: Internal documents obtained by Axios' Cuneyt Dil demonstrate the scale of Trump's project, which includes $24.7 million to upgrade the Concert Hall , a "Front of the House Renewal" and plumbing and elevator refurbishments. Still, as the administration casts Trump as the Kennedy Center's savior, the Washington Post reported Tuesday that ticket sales and fundraising fell after it adopted Trump's name. events.title: Windows on Arm app ecosystem expands across key workloads
events.summary: Expanding the Windows on Arm app ecosystem across key workloads Klaus Diaconu, Partner Director, Product Management, Windows Silicon & System Integration In a significant milestone for the platform, Microsoft and NVIDIA recently announced NVIDIA RTX Spark . These new devices are the most powerful and efficient, thin-and-light Windows PC ever, built with the Arm architecture. In the fall of 2026, devices from Microsoft Surface, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and MSI will be available. NVIDIA’s entry into the Windows on Arm silicon family joins the Qualcomm Snapdragon X series of chipsets that have already established Windows on Arm as the premium experience across Microsoft Surface Copilot+ PCs. The market is sending a clear signal: more silicon providers and more OEM partners are investing in Windows on Arm because customer demand is growing for these powerful and efficient Windows devices and experiences. Alongside the expanding PC landscape, the Windows app ecosystem continues to grow rapidly. As powerful Arm-based devices reach more customers, this motivates developers to build and optimize for the platform. Consequently, as the app catalog grows, customers have even more reason to choose Windows on Arm hardware. That virtuous cycle is now clearly in motion. The app catalog growth is evident in the Works on Windows on Arm site. This site catalogs over 7000 verified apps and games available for Windows on Arm and is built with compatibility data from Microsoft. Given the breadth of Arm-capable hardware available from multiple silicon providers and the depth of the app catalog, Windows on Arm has become a first-class platform for any workload. App Assure , Microsoft’s app compatibility program, with its dedicated Arm Advisory Service , continues to expand the Windows on Arm ecosystem. We continue working side by side with a diverse set of software development companies to bring their apps to the Windows on Arm catalog, ensuring that no customer is left behind. The goal of this blog is to share App Assure’s latest progress report: a roundup of some of the most notable new additions to the Windows on Arm app portfolio since our previous update . This i s a rapidly expanding category that demands its own section. Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) as wel l as education tools all play a critical role in how people learn in classrooms, research environments, or v ia independent study. As Windows on Arm devices become more prevalent, developers in this space now re cogniz e the op portunity to reach learners and professionals who value portable, power-efficient devices without sacrificing performance. The growing number of STEM and education apps now available reflects increasing investment aligned with these needs and the growing adoption of Windows on Arm devices by e duc ational cus tomers . Security remains foundational for Windows customers, and it spans far more than a single tool or workload. Modern environments require layered protection across endpoints, consistent device management, and secure connectivity, especially as work increasingly happens across hybrid, mobile, and distributed environments. Arm-based devices are designed with security at the core, integrating hardware, firmware, and software protections to help defend against modern threats. In addition to the built-in security features, strong support for Windows on Arm in endpoint protection, endpoint management, VPN and Zero Trust solutions helps ensure that customers can adopt these devices without compromising their security posture. Our previous update showcased well-known apps from companies including Norton, CrowdStrike, and McAfee in the Endpoint Protection space; VMware, Beyond Trust, and Cisco in the Endpoint Management space; and Nord, Zscaler, and Palo Alto Networks in the VPN and Zero Trust space. The continued expansion of the Windows on Arm security app ecosystem, as seen below, highlights how software vendors are aligning with customer expectations for secure, manageable Arm ‑ based deployments. Productivity apps remain the cornerstone of how people get work done on Windows. Whether managing projects, collaborating with teammates, organizing information, or communicating across teams, these apps are essential to our customers’ daily work. The growing list of productivity apps now available reflects both customer demand and increasing momentum from developers building with Arm as a first-class Windows platform. The new apps listed below join those previously announced from industry leaders such as Google, Adobe, Slack, Trello, and Dropbox. Creativity, social media and entertainment apps Windows devices are as important for work as they are for expression, connection and entertainment. From creative tools to social platforms and media experiences, these apps enable users to create, share and unwind throughout their day. Developers continue to bring rich, engaging experiences to Arm-based devices, ensuring users don’t have to choose between productivity and creativity. Our previous update saw brands such as Camtasia, Blender and Figma release Arm apps. Below are the latest additions. The takeaway is clear: Windows on Arm is no longer defined by potential, but by a rapidly expanding ecosystem of devices with apps available across workloads that customers depend on most. As developers continue to invest in Arm-native experiences and compatibility, customers gain more choices, flexibility, and confidence in adopting the next generation of Windows devices. As the ecosystem continues to expand, the Microsoft App Assure team is ready to assist software developers interested in bringing their apps to Windows on Arm. Through our Arm Advisory Service , we offer expert guidance, technical workshops, code samples, and an escalation path to Microsoft engineers ready to assist with software development. Reach out to us here to learn more. Finally, don’t forget to bookmark https://worksonwoa.com/ for a comprehensive and continuously updated list of all the apps available on Windows on Arm devices. events.summary: Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% percent on around $20 billion worth of US products , in an expanding trade war between the erstwhile allies.
